papers.conclusion: This work shows how induction heads emerge in an ICL task and paves the way for a better theoretical understanding of transformer learning dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
The weight matrices of an induction head have a simple structure described by three pseudo-parameters (α3, β2, γ3).
Training dynamics remain constrained to a 19-dimensional subspace, and only three dimensions are necessary for the induction head to emerge.
The emergence time of the induction head is quadratic in the context length (Θ(N^2)).
The three parameters emerge in a specific order: γ first, then β, then α.
The emergence of the induction head is self-contained, unaided by the other parameters.
papers.limitation:
Architectural scope is limited to a disentangled, attention-only transformer; production models with LayerNorm, MLPs, and additive residual streams may have different dynamics.
Theoretical results assume orthonormal inputs and zero initialization, which may not hold in practice and could alter emergence times.
The study uses a simplified ICL task (exact matching of item-label pairs), not natural language with its complexities.
future_direction: Exploring how data distributional properties like burstiness modulate the effective context length and emergence.
Investigating other means of reducing effective context length, such as special positional embeddings.
Applying a similar approach to study other phenomena like the in-context vs. in-weights learning trade-off, abrupt learning, or other transformer circuits.
papers.abstract: Transformers have become the dominant architecture for natural language processing. Part of their success is owed to a remarkable capability known as in-context learning (ICL): they can acquire and apply novel associations solely from their input context, without any updates to their weights. In this work, we study the emergence of induction heads, a previously identified mechanism in two-layer transformers that is particularly important for in-context learning. We uncover a relatively simple and interpretable structure of the weight matrices implementing the induction head. We theoretically explain the origin of this structure using a minimal ICL task formulation and a modified transformer architecture. We give a formal proof that the training dynamics remain constrained to a 19-dimensional subspace of the parameter space. Empirically, we validate this constraint while observing that only 3 dimensions account for the emergence of an induction head. By further studying the training dynamics inside this 3-dimensional subspace, we find that the time until the emergence of an induction head follows a tight asymptotic bound that is quadratic in the input context length.

papers.title: Toward Mechanistic Explanation of Deductive Reasoning in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does a small language model solve a deductive reasoning task, and what internal mechanisms (e.g., induction heads) are involved in implementing the logical inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a small language model can learn deductive reasoning by implementing rule-based circuits, with induction heads playing a central role, and introduces a truncated pseudoinverse technique for decoding query, key, and value information.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that a tiny LM can learn deductive reasoning by implementing symbolic rule-based circuits, with induction heads being a fundamental component, and suggests that induction heads may also be central in more complex logical reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
A simplified NanoGPT model trained with Chain-of-Thought can learn deductive reasoning rules and generalize to unseen examples.
Induction heads are crucial for implementing rule completion and rule chaining steps in the logical inference.
The model learns the underlying inference rules rather than memorizing patterns.
A single attention head can host multiple induction heads and other circuits, simplifying post-hoc explanation.
Training without Chain-of-Thought leads to memorization and poor generalization, indicating the importance of CoT for learning rules.
papers.limitation:
The interpretability techniques used (e.g., residual stream decoding and truncated pseudoinverse) are not 100% precise and may fail to decode the expected tokens.
The deductive reasoning task is simple and does not reflect the complexity of real-world logical reasoning.
future_direction: Investigating whether one-layer circuits resembling induction heads can be created by modifying the attention mechanism to decouple key and value positions.
Exploring the role of induction heads in solving more complex logical problems with larger language models.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have demonstrated relevant capabilities in solving problems that require logical reasoning; however, the corresponding internal mechanisms remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we show that a small language model can solve a deductive reasoning task by learning the underlying rules (rather than operating as a statistical learner). A low-level explanation of its internal representations and computational circuits is then provided. Our findings reveal that induction heads play a central role in the implementation of the rule completion and rule chaining steps involved in the logical inference required by the task.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence in environmental and Earth system sciences: explainability and trustworthiness
papers.research_question: What is the current state of XAI applications in environmental and Earth system sciences, and how does XAI contribute to trust in AI?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive review of 575 articles on explainable AI (XAI) applications in environmental and Earth system sciences, highlighting a critical gap between the use of XAI methods and the scientific investigation of trust in AI.
papers.conclusion: The review underlines the need for more studies on how to strengthen trust in AI applications and recommends developing a 'human-centered' XAI framework that incorporates the views and needs of multiple stakeholder groups for trustworthy decision-making.
papers.key_findings:
XAI applications are popular in various environmental domains including ecology, engineering, geology, remote sensing, and water resources.
SHAP and Shapley methods are the most popular XAI methods (135 articles), followed by feature importance, partial dependence plots, and LIME.
Only 1.2% of the reviewed studies (7 articles) addressed trustworthiness as a core research objective.
There is a critical knowledge gap in understanding the relationship between explainability and trust in AI for environmental decision-making.
While XAI applications continue to grow, they do not necessarily enhance trust, and more studies on strengthening trust are needed.
future_direction: More studies on how to strengthen trust in AI applications.
Developing human-centered XAI frameworks for trustworthy decision-making.
Adapting XAI methods for spatial and temporal data in environmental sciences.
papers.abstract: Abstract Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) methods have recently emerged to gain insights into complex machine learning models. XAI can be promising for environmental and Earth system science because high-stakes decision-making for management and planning requires justification based on evidence and systems understanding. However, an overview of XAI applications and trust in AI in environmental and Earth system science is still missing. To close this gap, we reviewed 575 articles. XAI applications are popular in various domains, including ecology, engineering, geology, remote sensing, water resources, meteorology, atmospheric sciences, geochemistry, and geophysics. XAI applications focused primarily on understanding and predicting anthropogenic changes in geospatial patterns and impacts on human society and natural resources, especially biological species distributions, vegetation, air quality, transportation, and climate-water related topics, including risk and management. Among XAI methods, the SHAP and Shapley methods were the most popular (135 articles), followed by feature importance (27), partial dependence plots (22), LIME (21), and saliency maps (15). Although XAI methods are often argued to increase trust in model predictions, only seven studies (1.2%) addressed trustworthiness as a core research objective. This gap is critical because understanding the relationship between explainability and trust is lacking. While XAI applications continue to grow, they do not necessarily enhance trust. Hence, more studies on how to strengthen trust in AI applications are critically needed. Finally, this review underlines the recommendation of developing a “human-centered” XAI framework that incorporates the distinct views and needs of multiple stakeholder groups to enable trustworthy decision-making.

papers.title: Sparse Reward Subsystem in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Does there exist a sparse reward subsystem in LLM hidden states analogous to the biological reward subsystem, and what are its properties?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a sparse reward subsystem in LLM hidden states, consisting of value neurons that encode state value and dopamine neurons that encode reward prediction error, and shows their critical role in reasoning and their robustness across models and tasks.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess a sparse reward subsystem analogous to the biological reward subsystem, which is consistent across tasks, layers, model scales, and architectures, and has potential applications.
papers.key_findings:
Value neurons exist in LLM hidden states and can predict the value of the current state using only a small fraction of neurons.
Ablating even 1% of value neurons severely impairs reasoning performance, while random ablation does not.
Value neurons are robust across diverse datasets, model scales, layers, and architectural designs.
Value neurons are transferable across different datasets and across models fine-tuned from the same base model.
Dopamine neurons exist and encode reward prediction error, with activation patterns correlating with positive and negative surprises.
papers.limitation: Dopamine neurons are demonstrated primarily through case studies rather than quantitative metrics.
future_direction: Further explore applications of the reward subsystem for detecting and guiding LLM generation and reasoning.
Develop quantitative metrics for measuring dopamine neurons.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we identify a sparse reward subsystem within the hidden states of Large Language Models (LLMs), drawing an analogy to the biological reward subsystem in the human brain. We demonstrate that this subsystem contains value neurons that represent the model's internal expectation of state value, and through intervention experiments, we establish the importance of these neurons for reasoning. Our experiments reveal that these value neurons are robust across diverse datasets, model scales, and architectures; furthermore, they exhibit significant transferability across different datasets and models fine-tuned from the same base model. By examining cases where value predictions and actual rewards diverge, we identify dopamine neurons within the reward subsystem which encode reward prediction errors (RPE). These neurons exhibit high activation when the reward is higher than expected and low activation when the reward is lower than expected.

papers.title: How Transformers Get Rich: Approximation and Dynamics Analysis
papers.research_question: How do transformers implement induction heads, both in terms of approximation and learning dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides theoretical analysis showing how two-layer transformers can approximate induction heads and characterizes the training dynamics with a sharp transition from n-gram to induction head learning.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can efficiently implement induction heads through specific roles of submodules, and learning induction heads involves a sharp transition from n-gram mechanisms driven by time-scale separation and component proportions.
papers.key_findings:
Two-layer single-head transformers without FFNs can approximate vanilla induction heads.
Two-layer multi-head transformers without FFNs can approximate generalized induction heads (in-context n-gram).
Two-layer multi-head transformers with FFNs can approximate generalized induction heads with generic similarity functions.
Training dynamics on a mixed target show a sharp transition from 4-gram to induction head, with four phases.
The transition is driven by time-scale separation in self-attention and speed differences due to component proportions.
papers.limitation:
Extending analysis to rotary positional encoding may be nontrivial.
Dynamics analysis is limited to a simple mixed target without FFNs.
future_direction: Extending analysis to rotary positional encoding.
Generalizing dynamics analysis to nonlinear functions with FFNs.
papers.abstract: Transformers have demonstrated exceptional in-context learning capabilities, yet the theoretical understanding of the underlying mechanisms remains limited. A recent work (Elhage et al., 2021) identified a ``rich'' in-context mechanism known as induction head, contrasting with ``lazy'' $n$-gram models that overlook long-range dependencies. In this work, we provide both approximation and dynamics analyses of how transformers implement induction heads. In the {\em approximation} analysis, we formalize both standard and generalized induction head mechanisms, and examine how transformers can efficiently implement them, with an emphasis on the distinct role of each transformer submodule. For the {\em dynamics} analysis, we study the training dynamics on a synthetic mixed target, composed of a 4-gram and an in-context 2-gram component. This controlled setting allows us to precisely characterize the entire training process and uncover an {\em abrupt transition} from lazy (4-gram) to rich (induction head) mechanisms as training progresses.

papers.title: Triple Phase Transitions: Understanding the Learning Dynamics of Large Language Models from a Neuroscience Perspective
papers.research_question: How do phase transitions in large language model training manifest in terms of alignment with human brain activity, internal representations, and downstream task performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies three common phase transitions in LLM training: an initial alignment with the brain when instruction following emerges, a detachment during task performance stagnation, and a realignment when tasks are consolidated.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that LLM learning involves three phase transitions that synchronize brain alignment, internal representations, and task performance, providing a multi-scale view of emergent abilities.
papers.key_findings:
Phase 1 (Brain Alignment and Instruction Following): Alignment with the entire brain surges as LLMs begin adhering to task instructions.
Phase 2 (Brain Detachment and Stagnation): LLMs diverge from the brain during a period of downstream task accuracy stagnation.
Phase 3 (Brain Realignment and Consolidation): Alignment with the brain reoccurs as LLMs become capable of solving downstream tasks.
These three phase transitions are observed across LLMs with distinct architectures and training data.
The transitions only occur when the input language matches a language sufficiently represented in the model's training corpus.
papers.limitation: The brain encoding accuracy and intrinsic dimensionality are not perfectly congruent, leaving open questions about what aspects of activation changes are not captured by intrinsic dimensionality alone.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit abrupt emergent behavior, whereby new abilities arise at certain points during their training. This phenomenon, commonly referred to as a ''phase transition'', remains poorly understood. In this study, we conduct an integrative analysis of such phase transitions by examining three interconnected perspectives: the similarity between LLMs and the human brain, the internal states of LLMs, and downstream task performance. We propose a novel interpretation for the learning dynamics of LLMs that vary in both training data and architecture, revealing that three phase transitions commonly emerge across these models during training: (1) alignment with the entire brain surges as LLMs begin adhering to task instructions Brain Alignment and Instruction Following, (2) unexpectedly, LLMs diverge from the brain during a period in which downstream task accuracy temporarily stagnates Brain Detachment and Stagnation, and (3) alignment with the brain reoccurs as LLMs become capable of solving the downstream tasks Brain Realignment and Consolidation. These findings illuminate the underlying mechanisms of phase transitions in LLMs, while opening new avenues for interdisciplinary research bridging AI and neuroscience.

papers.title: Systematic Evaluation of Single-Cell Foundation Model Interpretability Reveals Attention Captures Co-Expression Rather Than Unique Regulatory Signal
papers.research_question: Does attention in single-cell foundation models capture causal regulatory relationships or just co-expression? Do attention-derived edge scores provide incremental value beyond gene-level features for predicting perturbation outcomes?
papers.core_contribution: Attention patterns in single-cell foundation models encode structured biological information (e.g., protein-protein interactions in early layers, transcriptional regulation in late layers) but do not capture causal regulatory signal; they provide no incremental value over gene-level features for predicting perturbation outcomes.
papers.conclusion: Attention patterns in single-cell foundation models capture co-expression rather than causal regulatory signal, and the proposed evaluation framework provides a reusable quality-control standard for mechanistic interpretability in this domain.
papers.key_findings:
Attention patterns show layer-specific biological specialization but do not outperform trivial gene-level baselines for perturbation prediction.
Pairwise edge scores (attention or correlation) provide no incremental predictive value beyond gene-level features.
Causal ablation of 'regulatory' attention heads does not degrade perturbation prediction, indicating distributed redundancy.
The relationship between attention and correlation is context-dependent across cell types and perturbation modalities.
Cell-State Stratified Interpretability (CSSI) improves attention-derived GRN recovery by controlling for heterogeneity.
papers.limitation:
Causal ablation only performed on Geneformer V2-316M, not on scGPT due to architectural differences.
Perturbation data limited to four cell types and two modalities; additional tissues, species, and architectures remain untested.
No decisive positive control demonstrates recovery of known causal regulatory structure in a realistic perturbation setting.
future_direction: Test additional tissues, species, and architectures (e.g., scFoundation).
Focus interpretability efforts on residual-stream geometry, MLP-stored knowledge, or representations from the full forward pass.
papers.abstract: We present a systematic evaluation framework - thirty-seven analyses, 153 statistical tests, four cell types, two perturbation modalities - for assessing mechanistic interpretability in single-cell foundation models. Applying this framework to scGPT and Geneformer, we find that attention patterns encode structured biological information with layer-specific organisation - protein-protein interactions in early layers, transcriptional regulation in late layers - but this structure provides no incremental value for perturbation prediction: trivial gene-level baselines outperform both attention and correlation edges (AUROC 0.81-0.88 versus 0.70), pairwise edge scores add zero predictive contribution, and causal ablation of regulatory heads produces no degradation. These findings generalise from K562 to RPE1 cells; the attention-correlation relationship is context-dependent, but gene-level dominance is universal. Cell-State Stratified Interpretability (CSSI) addresses an attention-specific scaling failure, improving GRN recovery up to 1.85x. The framework establishes reusable quality-control standards for the field.

papers.title: Position: Solve Layerwise Linear Models First to Understand Neural Dynamical Phenomena (Neural Collapse, Emergence, Lazy/Rich Regime, and Grokking)
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the dynamical feedback principle as a unifying explanation for neural dynamical phenomena (neural collapse, emergence, lazy/rich regimes, grokking) and advocates for prioritizing the study of layerwise linear models to accelerate deep learning science.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that layerwise linear models, through the dynamical feedback principle, capture essential dynamics of DNNs and should be prioritized to advance theoretical understanding and accelerate the science of deep learning.
papers.key_findings:
Sigmoidal dynamics in diagonal linear neural networks cause delayed saturation and stage-like training, explaining emergence and scaling laws.
Greedy dynamics in linear neural networks prioritize salient features, leading to low-rank bias and neural collapse.
Layer imbalance (λ-balanced condition) controls the transition between lazy (linear) and rich (nonlinear) dynamics.
Grokking can be understood as a transition from lazy to rich dynamics, controllable by layer imbalance and weight-to-target ratio.
The dynamical feedback principle unifies these phenomena as consequences of layerwise structure dynamics.
future_direction: Investigate the connection between greedy dynamics and generalization.
Develop techniques to encourage greedy dynamics during training.
Explore the limits of layerwise linear models and extend the principle to more complex architectures.
papers.abstract: In physics, complex systems are often simplified into minimal, solvable models that retain only the core principles. In machine learning, layerwise linear models (e.g., linear neural networks) act as simplified representations of neural network dynamics. These models follow the dynamical feedback principle, which describes how layers mutually govern and amplify each other's evolution. This principle extends beyond the simplified models, successfully explaining a wide range of dynamical phenomena in deep neural networks, including neural collapse, emergence, lazy and rich regimes, and grokking. In this position paper, we call for the use of layerwise linear models retaining the core principles of neural dynamical phenomena to accelerate the science of deep learning.

papers.title: High-dimensional manifold of solutions in neural networks: insights from statistical physics
papers.core_contribution: The paper reviews the statistical mechanics approach to neural networks, focusing on the perceptron model, and explains how the geometry of the solution space (manifold of solutions) changes with the size of the training set.
papers.key_findings:
The SAT/UNSAT transition separates a satisfiable phase where solutions exist from an unsatisfiable phase where the solution set is empty.
In the binary perceptron, typical solutions are isolated, but there exist subdominant, wide flat minima that are algorithmically accessible.
The local entropy transition marks a change in the geometry of solution regions and is connected to the onset of algorithmic hardness in binary models.
In the spherical negative perceptron, the solution space is star-shaped, with a kernel region from which any other solution can be reached via a zero-error geodesic path.
Linear mode connectivity between solutions can be characterized analytically, revealing the structure of the solution manifold.
papers.abstract: In these pedagogic notes I review the statistical mechanics approach to neural networks, focusing on the paradigmatic example of the perceptron architecture with binary an continuous weights, in the classification setting. I will review the Gardner's approach based on replica method and the derivation of the SAT/UNSAT transition in the storage setting. Then, I discuss some recent works that unveiled how the zero training error configurations are geometrically arranged, and how this arrangement changes as the size of the training set increases. I also illustrate how different regions of solution space can be explored analytically and how the landscape in the vicinity of a solution can be characterized. I give evidence how, in binary weight models, algorithmic hardness is a consequence of the disappearance of a clustered region of solutions that extends to very large distances. Finally, I demonstrate how the study of linear mode connectivity between solutions can give insights into the average shape of the solution manifold.

papers.title: A Survey on Mechanistic Interpretability for Multi-Modal Foundation Models
papers.research_question: How can LLM interpretability methods be adapted to multimodal foundation models, and what are the mechanistic differences between unimodal and multimodal systems?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a comprehensive survey of mechanistic interpretability for multimodal foundation models, introducing a taxonomy and comparing insights between unimodal and multimodal models to highlight research gaps.
papers.conclusion: The survey reviews mechanistic understanding methods for MMFMs, introduces a taxonomy differentiating interpretability methods adapted from language models and those designed for multimodal models, and compares mechanistic insights to identify gaps and their impact on downstream applications.
papers.key_findings:
LLM-based interpretability methods can be extended to MMFMs with moderate adjustments, particularly when treating visual and textual inputs similarly.
Novel multimodal challenges arise such as interpreting visual embeddings in human-understandable terms, necessitating new dedicated analysis methods.
While interpretability aids downstream tasks, applications like hallucination mitigation and model editing remain underdeveloped in multimodal models compared to language models.
There is a substantial gap between the interpretability of LLMs and MMFMs, with a lack of unified benchmarks and tools for multimodal interpretability.
The survey proposes a three-dimensional taxonomy for mechanistic interpretability in multimodal models based on model family, interpretability techniques, and applications.
papers.limitation:
The survey mainly focuses on image-text multimodal models without considering other modalities such as video, time series, or 3D.
The survey does not contain experimental analysis because of the lack of unified benchmarks.
The survey only focuses on transformer-based or diffusion models, without considering novel model architectures such as MAMBA.
future_direction: Extending mechanistic interpretability techniques to analyze unified vision-text understanding and generation models.
Developing sequential batch model editing techniques for multimodal models, including diffusion and multimodal language models.
Exploring the effectiveness of sparse autoencoders and their variants for controlling and steering multimodal models.
papers.abstract: The rise of foundation models has transformed machine learning research, prompting efforts to uncover their inner workings and develop more efficient and reliable applications for better control. While significant progress has been made in interpreting Large Language Models (LLMs), multimodal foundation models (MMFMs) - such as contrastive vision-language models, generative vision-language models, and text-to-image models - pose unique interpretability challenges beyond unimodal frameworks. Despite initial studies, a substantial gap remains between the interpretability of LLMs and MMFMs. This survey explores two key aspects: (1) the adaptation of LLM interpretability methods to multimodal models and (2) understanding the mechanistic differences between unimodal language models and crossmodal systems. By systematically reviewing current MMFM analysis techniques, we propose a structured taxonomy of interpretability methods, compare insights across unimodal and multimodal architectures, and highlight critical research gaps.

papers.title: Interpretable Neural Networks based classifiers for categorical inputs
papers.research_question: How can we interpret the output of neural network classifiers that take categorical inputs by expanding the network's function as a sum of contributions from input patterns?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method to interpret neural network classifiers for categorical inputs by expanding the network's output function as a polynomial sum of contributions from input patterns, which can be interpreted as an energy model and related to maximum entropy models.
papers.conclusion: The method provides a global interpretation of neural network classifiers for categorical inputs, and lower-order terms often dominate, allowing for approximate interpretations. The method can be extended to real-valued inputs with approximations.
papers.key_findings:
The output of a neural network classifier with categorical inputs can be exactly represented as a finite polynomial expansion.
The coefficients of the expansion can be computed via derivatives or perturbations at the zero input.
Applying an Ising gauge transformation emphasizes lower-order terms.
In the MNIST example, first and second order terms capture most of the network's behavior.
In the protein sequence prediction, first order terms are often sufficient, but second order terms can improve predictions and reveal three-body interactions.
papers.limitation: The method is exact only for categorical inputs and for networks with C∞ activation functions; for real-valued inputs the expansion is infinite and only approximate.
future_direction: Apply the technique to the study of protein sequences.
Extend the method to real-valued inputs for approximate interpretations.
Investigate robustness to adversarial attacks using the reduced description.
papers.abstract: Because of the pervasive usage of Neural Networks in human sensitive applications, their interpretability is becoming an increasingly important topic in machine learning. In this work we introduce a simple way to interpret the output function of a neural network classifier that take as input categorical variables. By exploiting a mapping between a neural network classifier and a physical energy model, we show that in these cases each layer of the network, and the logits layer in particular, can be expanded as a sum of terms that account for the contribution to the classification of each input pattern. For instance, at the first order, the expansion considers just the linear relation between input features and output while at the second order pairwise dependencies between input features are also accounted for. The analysis of the contributions of each pattern, after an appropriate gauge transformation, is presented in two cases where the effectiveness of the method can be appreciated.

papers.title: Toy Models of Superposition
papers.research_question: Why do neurons sometimes align with interpretable features and sometimes not, and how can neural networks represent more features than they have dimensions (superposition)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that superposition—where neural networks store more sparse features than dimensions—is a real phenomenon, explains polysemanticity, and reveals a phase change and geometric structure in feature representations.
papers.conclusion: Superposition occurs in neural networks, allowing them to represent more features than dimensions, which has important implications for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Superposition is a real, observed phenomenon in neural networks.
Both monosemantic and polysemantic neurons can form.
At least some kinds of computation can be performed in superposition.
Whether features are stored in superposition is governed by a phase change.
Superposition organizes features into geometric structures such as digons, triangles, pentagons, and tetrahedrons.
papers.limitation:
The toy models are simple and it is unclear what to generalize to real networks.
The ReLU hidden layer toy model has a weakness where the model circumvents the activation function if possible.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often pack many unrelated concepts into a single neuron - a puzzling phenomenon known as 'polysemanticity' which makes interpretability much more challenging. This paper provides a toy model where polysemanticity can be fully understood, arising as a result of models storing additional sparse features in "superposition." We demonstrate the existence of a phase change, a surprising connection to the geometry of uniform polytopes, and evidence of a link to adversarial examples. We also discuss potential implications for mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Explaining the Explainer: Understanding the Inner Workings of Transformer-based Symbolic Regression Models
papers.research_question: How can we understand the internal mechanisms of transformer-based symbolic regression models, specifically by identifying circuits responsible for generating symbolic operators?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PATCHES, a novel evolutionary circuit discovery algorithm for symbolic regression transformers, and establishes a formal evaluation framework (faithfulness, completeness, minimality) for circuit correctness.
papers.conclusion: This work establishes symbolic regression as a promising domain for mechanistic interpretability and provides a principled methodology for circuit discovery in such models.
papers.key_findings:
PATCHES successfully isolates circuits for specific symbolic operators (e.g., sin, add, log) in a transformer-based SR model.
Mean patching combined with functional evaluation (accuracy) is more reliable for discovering correct circuits than resample patching or model-based (logit) evaluation.
Direct logit attribution and probing classifiers primarily capture correlational features, limiting their utility for causal circuit discovery.
Circuits for SR are dense (40-78% of model components), attributed to the small vocabulary and complex syntactic encoding required.
papers.limitation:
Resample patching sometimes fails to sufficiently suppress the target token's information, hindering causal isolation and circuit discovery.
High baseline performance for some operators (e.g., addition) makes it difficult to achieve completeness, as patching does not degrade performance enough.
papers.abstract: Following their success across many domains, transformers have also proven effective for symbolic regression (SR); however, the internal mechanisms underlying their generation of mathematical operators remain largely unexplored. Although mechanistic interpretability has successfully identified circuits in language and vision models, it has not yet been applied to SR. In this article, we introduce PATCHES, an evolutionary circuit discovery algorithm that identifies compact and correct circuits for SR. Using PATCHES, we isolate 28 circuits, providing the first circuit-level characterisation of an SR transformer. We validate these findings through a robust causal evaluation framework based on key notions such as faithfulness, completeness, and minimality. Our analysis shows that mean patching with performance-based evaluation most reliably isolates functionally correct circuits. In contrast, we demonstrate that direct logit attribution and probing classifiers primarily capture correlational features rather than causal ones, limiting their utility for circuit discovery. Overall, these results establish SR as a high-potential application domain for mechanistic interpretability and propose a principled methodology for circuit discovery.

papers.title: On the Symmetries of Deep Learning Models and their Internal Representations
papers.research_question: How do the symmetries of a network architecture (via intertwiner groups) relate to the symmetries in the network's internal representations of data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces intertwiner groups to connect architectural symmetries with symmetries in internal representations, and shows that for ReLU networks, the activation basis is special for interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that intertwiner groups connect architectural symmetries to representation symmetries, and provide a justification for focusing on activation basis in ReLU networks for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Intertwiner groups describe weight space symmetries and propagate to symmetries in internal representations.
Stitching with GReLU transformations incurs a small accuracy penalty, indicating that much of the variation between networks can be accounted for by GReLU.
GReLU-Procrustes and GReLU-CKA are effective dissimilarity measures invariant to GReLU transformations.
For ReLU networks, interpretability is higher in the activation basis than in arbitrary linear combinations, but this is not the case for networks without ReLU.
papers.limitation:
The theory does not fully account for residual connections, as noted in remark 3.6.
Stitching with GReLU does not achieve full accuracy, indicating that internal representations are not perfectly aligned by permutations and scalings.
papers.abstract: Symmetry is a fundamental tool in the exploration of a broad range of complex systems. In machine learning symmetry has been explored in both models and data. In this paper we seek to connect the symmetries arising from the architecture of a family of models with the symmetries of that family's internal representation of data. We do this by calculating a set of fundamental symmetry groups, which we call the intertwiner groups of the model. We connect intertwiner groups to a model's internal representations of data through a range of experiments that probe similarities between hidden states across models with the same architecture. Our work suggests that the symmetries of a network are propagated into the symmetries in that network's representation of data, providing us with a better understanding of how architecture affects the learning and prediction process. Finally, we speculate that for ReLU networks, the intertwiner groups may provide a justification for the common practice of concentrating model interpretability exploration on the activation basis in hidden layers rather than arbitrary linear combinations thereof.

papers.title: To Sink or Not to Sink: Visual Information Pathways in Large Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the fundamental benefits of ViT attention sink tokens in large vision-language models, and how can they be understood and operationalized to improve visual reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes ViT attention sinks in LVLMs, finding they encode high-level semantic context, and introduces DIYSink, a framework that dynamically leverages these sinks to improve visual reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: ViT attention sinks are important carriers of high-level visual context and can be effectively leveraged, both via training-free and training-based methods, to enhance the visual reasoning capabilities of large vision-language models.
papers.key_findings:
ViT sink tokens propagate into the LLM, activating distinct hidden dimensions different from LLM-emerged sinks.
ViT sinks capture coarse-grained, high-level contextual features and are semantically meaningful.
ViT sinks are beneficial for global tasks requiring high-level understanding but can degrade performance on local, detail-rich tasks.
A simple training-free approach (sink-to-the-front) improves performance across various LVLMs.
The proposed DIYSink framework, with dual MLP projectors and dynamic token selection, yields substantial improvements across a range of benchmarks.
papers.limitation: The proposed DIYSink framework requires access to training data and computational resources for training from scratch.
future_direction: Extending DIYSink to other modalities such as video and audio.
papers.abstract: Large Vision Language Models (LVLMs) have recently emerged as powerful architectures capable of understanding and reasoning over both visual and textual information. These models typically rely on two key components: a Vision Transformer (ViT) and a Large Language Model (LLM). ViT encodes visual content into a sequence of image tokens and serves as the perceptual front-end -- the eyes of the model. In contrast, the LLM interprets these tokens to perform high-level reasoning, generates responses, and functions as the cognitive core -- the brain of the model. However, it remains unclear which visual tokens contribute most significantly to understanding and reasoning, and how effectively these signals are propagated from ViT to the LLM. While most existing works have focused on identifying attention sinks, low-semantic tokens receiving disproportionately high attention, within the LLM, we shift the focus to the vision encoder by identifying a class of high-norm visual tokens from ViT, referred to as ViT attention sinks -- a problem that has been rarely studied but is indeed very important for LVLMs. Our findings show that these ViT sinks encapsulate high-level semantic concepts from images, allowing the LLM to perform more effective understanding and reasoning. Despite their importance, these sink tokens are often overlooked in existing LVLM architectures. To explore their contribution, we present both qualitative and quantitative analyses of the information embedded in these sink tokens. We also propose both training-free and training-based approaches to better leverage how this information is interpreted by the LLM, and to what extent. By explicitly utilizing these tokens, we demonstrate substantial improvements across a range of LVLMs and visual reasoning tasks, highlighting the untapped potential of ViT attention sinks in enhancing visual reasoning.

papers.title: Explainable deep learning for rainfall prediction: A CNN-XGBoost hybrid approach in the northern region of Bangladesh
papers.research_question: This paper investigates the application of deep learning models for rainfall prediction in the northern region of Bangladesh, focusing on the comparative performance of six models and the interpretability of a proposed hybrid model.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a hybrid CNN-XGBoost model for rainfall prediction that consistently outperforms other models (CNN, LSTM, XGB, Ensemble, Transformer-XGB) across two distinct datasets and provides interpretability of its decisions using SHAP.
papers.conclusion: The CNN-XGB hybrid model provides accurate and consistent rainfall predictions for the northern region of Bangladesh, outperforming other models, and the use of SHAP enhances model transparency and trust for practical applications like urban planning and disaster management.
papers.key_findings:
The CNN-XGB hybrid model achieved the lowest RMSE (0.65 mm/day) and MAE (0.28 mm/day) and highest R2 (0.99) on the satellite dataset for Rajshahi district.
On the ground dataset, the CNN-XGB model also performed best for Rajshahi district with RMSE of 16.28 mm/month, MAE of 7.85 mm/month, and R2 of 0.98.
The satellite dataset with 16 meteorological variables led to better model performance than the ground dataset with only rainfall data.
SHAP analysis identified that engineered features (e.g., trends, rolling statistics, transformations of precipitation) and climatic variables were the most influential predictors.
The hybrid model effectively captures both spatial and temporal patterns in rainfall data, demonstrating robustness across different districts and data sources.
papers.limitation:
The ground dataset's monthly resolution restricts the model's ability to capture short-term rainfall variability.
Crucial environmental and urban factors such as soil moisture, land use, and topography were excluded due to data unavailability, which may affect localized accuracy.
future_direction: Explore domain adaptation to improve generalization across diverse regions.
Integrate multi-source data (e.g., radar observations, vegetation indices, satellite-derived soil moisture) to enhance robustness under varying climatic conditions.
Couple the proposed model with numerical weather prediction (NWP) models to refine forecasts by blending data-driven and physics-based approaches.
papers.abstract: Abstract Accurate precipitation forecasting is crucial for evaluating various hydrological processes. This research explores the application of deep learning models for rainfall prediction in the northern region of Bangladesh, focusing on the comparative performance of six models: CNN (Convolutional Neural Network), LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory), XGB (Extreme Gradient Boosting), Ensemble Model, Transformer-XGB, and CNN-XGB. Two distinct datasets were utilized to assess the effectiveness of these models. Among them, the CNN-XGB hybrid model consistently demonstrated superior performance across all evaluation metrics, establishing it as the most reliable predictor in this study. Rajshahi district’s satellite dataset showed an RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error) of 0.65 mm/day, MAE (Mean Absolute Error) of 0.28 mm/day, and R 2 of 0.99. In the ground dataset, Rajshahi district beat other models with an RMSE of 16.28 mm/month, MAE of 7.85 mm/month, and R 2 of 0.98. These findings demonstrate the model’s efficacy across several data sources. To enhance the interpretability of the proposed CNN-XGB model, we deployed the SHAP (Shapley Additive exPlanations) explainer, providing insights into the model’s decision-making process. This research highlights the potential of hybrid models in enhancing rainfall prediction accuracy while providing transparency through explainable AI techniques. Beyond hydrology, the predicted rainfall patterns provide essential inputs for urban planners to optimize land-use zoning in flood-prone areas, and guide resilient infrastructure development. Code Available: https://github.com/Shafi3397/Rainfall-Prediction-using-CNN-XGBoost

papers.title: Expressive dynamics models with nonlinear injective readouts enable reliable recovery of latent features from neural activity
papers.research_question: How can we learn interpretable latent dynamical systems from neural activity? The paper proposes that using injective nonlinear readouts in neural population dynamics models can prevent the model from inventing latent features not reflected in the data, leading to more interpretable dynamics.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ODIN, a neural population dynamics model with an injective nonlinear readout, which learns interpretable latent dynamical systems from neural activity by preventing the invention of misleading latent features and enabling accurate recovery of ground-truth dynamics.
papers.conclusion: ODIN is a promising method for distilling interpretable dynamics from neural activity, enabling better understanding of neural computation.
papers.key_findings:
ODIN with injective nonlinear readout recovers latent activity more accurately than linear or MLP readouts, especially when the latent dimensionality is overestimated.
Linear and MLP readouts tend to be non-injective, allowing latent features that do not affect neural activity, which degrades interpretability.
ODIN can recover nonlinear embeddings and fixed point structures from synthetic data.
On biological neural data, ODIN reconstructs neural activity with fewer latent dimensions than linear readout models and performs comparably to state-of-the-art methods.
papers.limitation:
ODIN is not yet able to account for inputs to the system that may be coming from areas that are not directly modeled, so it models the dynamics as an autonomous system.
Human neural interfaces combined with an understanding of neural computation might lead to strategies that are effective at influencing behavior, which could be misused.
future_direction: Developing methods for input inference in NODE-based models.
Focusing on applications of this research that are scientific and medical rather than commercial or political.
papers.abstract: The advent of large-scale neural recordings has enabled new methods to discover the computational mechanisms of neural circuits by understanding the rules that govern how their state evolves over time. While these \textit{neural dynamics} cannot be directly measured, they can typically be approximated by low-dimensional models in a latent space. How these models represent the mapping from latent space to neural space can affect the interpretability of the latent representation. We show that typical choices for this mapping (e.g., linear or MLP) often lack the property of injectivity, meaning that changes in latent state are not obligated to affect activity in the neural space. During training, non-injective readouts incentivize the invention of dynamics that misrepresent the underlying system and the computation it performs. Combining our injective Flow readout with prior work on interpretable latent dynamics models, we created the Ordinary Differential equations autoencoder with Injective Nonlinear readout (ODIN), which captures latent dynamical systems that are nonlinearly embedded into observed neural activity via an approximately injective nonlinear mapping. We show that ODIN can recover nonlinearly embedded systems from simulated neural activity, even when the nature of the system and embedding are unknown. Additionally, ODIN enables the unsupervised recovery of underlying dynamical features (e.g., fixed points) and embedding geometry. When applied to biological neural recordings, ODIN can reconstruct neural activity with comparable accuracy to previous state-of-the-art methods while using substantially fewer latent dimensions. Overall, ODIN's accuracy in recovering ground-truth latent features and ability to accurately reconstruct neural activity with low dimensionality make it a promising method for distilling interpretable dynamics that can help explain neural computation.

papers.title: Invertible Neural Networks for Understanding Semantics of Invariances of CNN Representations
papers.research_question: How can we understand the semantic concepts and invariances learned by deep neural networks (specifically CNNs) by recovering the invariances and translating the representations into an interpretable form without modifying the original model?
papers.core_contribution: An invertible neural network (INN) approach that recovers the invariances a deep model has learned and bijectively translates the model representation and its invariances into a semantically accessible encoding without compromising the original model's performance.
papers.conclusion: The invertible approach provides a powerful, post-hoc diagnostic pipeline for explaining deep representations by recovering invariances and enabling semantic interpretation without retraining the model.
papers.key_findings:
The method visualizes representations and their invariances without artifacts, outperforming existing network inversion methods.
Analysis of FaceNet shows that invariances (e.g., to pose) increase with layer depth, while some features (e.g., glasses) remain identity-relevant across layers.
The approach can quantify how much of a semantic concept (e.g., texture vs. shape) is captured by a model's representation, revealing biases like texture bias in ImageNet-trained CNNs.
Semantic modifications in the interpretable space correctly alter the original representation and can be visualized, enabling diagnostic probing of model sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Abstract To tackle increasingly complex tasks, it has become an essential ability of neural networks to learn abstract representations. These task-specific representations and, particularly, the invariances they capture turn neural networks into black-box models that lack interpretability. To open such a black box, it is, therefore, crucial to uncover the different semantic concepts a model has learned as well as those that it has learned to be invariant to. We present an approach based on invertible neural networks (INNs) that (i) recovers the task-specific, learned invariances by disentangling the remaining factor of variation in the data and that (ii) invertibly transforms these recovered invariances combined with the model representation into an equally expressive one with accessible semantic concepts. As a consequence, neural network representations become understandable by providing the means to (i) expose their semantic meaning, (ii) semantically modify a representation, and (iii) visualize individual learned semantic concepts and invariances. Our invertible approach significantly extends the abilities to understand black-box models by enabling post hoc interpretations of state-of-the-art networks without compromising their performance. Our implementation is available at https://compvis.github.io/invariances/ .

papers.title: LyTimeT: Towards Robust and Interpretable State-Variable Discovery
papers.research_question: How to extract true dynamical variables from high-dimensional video data robustly and interpretably, despite distracting visual factors such as background motion, occlusions, and texture changes?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LyTimeT, a two-phase framework that combines global spatio-temporal attention with Lyapunov-based stability regularization to learn robust, interpretable latent representations of dynamical systems from video.
papers.conclusion: LyTimeT bridges representation learning and stability theory, providing a principled foundation for robust, generalizable, and scientifically meaningful modeling of complex dynamical systems.
papers.key_findings:
LyTimeT achieves mutual information and intrinsic dimension estimates closest to ground truth compared to baselines like NSV and TIDE.
LyTimeT delivers the lowest analytical mean squared error among CNN-based and transformer-only baselines.
LyTimeT remains invariant under background perturbations, demonstrating robustness to nuisance variation.
Lyapunov regularization improves MI, lowers AMSE, and reduces long-horizon error, enhancing stability and interpretability.
LyTimeT-Lite variant maintains near-optimal performance with lower computational cost, suitable for real-time deployment.
future_direction: Incorporating physics-informed priors such as symplectic structures, conservation laws, or energy-preserving constraints.
Investigating hierarchical and sparse attention mechanisms to scale to higher-resolution videos and partially observed systems.
Exploring online or continual learning to adapt latent variables in evolving environments for closed-loop control applications.
papers.abstract: Extracting the true dynamical variables of a system from high-dimensional video is challenging due to distracting visual factors such as background motion, occlusions, and texture changes. We propose LyTimeT, a two-phase framework for interpretable variable extraction that learns robust and stable latent representations of dynamical systems. In Phase 1, LyTimeT employs a spatio-temporal TimeSformer-based autoencoder that uses global attention to focus on dynamically relevant regions while suppressing nuisance variation, enabling distraction-robust latent state learning and accurate long-horizon video prediction. In Phase 2, we probe the learned latent space, select the most physically meaningful dimensions using linear correlation analysis, and refine the transition dynamics with a Lyapunov-based stability regularizer to enforce contraction and reduce error accumulation during roll-outs. Experiments on five synthetic benchmarks and four real-world dynamical systems, including chaotic phenomena, show that LyTimeT achieves mutual information and intrinsic dimension estimates closest to ground truth, remains invariant under background perturbations, and delivers the lowest analytical mean squared error among CNN-based (TIDE) and transformer-only baselines. Our results demonstrate that combining spatio-temporal attention with stability constraints yields predictive models that are not only accurate but also physically interpretable.

papers.title: Tensor Product Decomposition Networks: Uncovering Representations of Structure Learned by Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How do neural networks encode compositional symbolic structure in their vector representations, and do they use tensor product representations?
papers.core_contribution: TPDNs show that RNNs can learn structured representations similar to tensor product representations for artificial tasks, but for real-world NLP tasks, representations are less structured, approximated by bag-of-words, suggesting training tasks may not induce robust structural representations.
papers.conclusion: RNNs trained on structure-sensitive tasks learn representations well approximated by tensor-product representations, but sentence encoders for NLP tasks show less structure, approximated by bag-of-words.
papers.key_findings:
TPDNs can closely approximate RNN representations for digit sequence copying tasks, indicating structured encoding.
Linear RNNs use bidirectional role schemes, while tree RNNs use tree position roles for representation.
For natural language processing models like InferSent and Skip-thought, representations are well approximated by bag-of-words, showing limited structure.
The nature of learned representations is related to the RNN's structure and the training task.
Training tasks influence whether networks discover structured or unstructured representations.
papers.abstract: We introduce an analysis technique for understanding compositional structure present in the vector representations used by neural networks. The inner workings of neural networks are notoriously difficult to understand, and in particular it is far from clear how they manage to perform remarkably well on tasks that depend on compositional structure even though they use continuous vector representations with no obvious compositional structure. Using our analysis technique, we show that the representations of these models can be closely approximated by Tensor Product Representations, a type of interpretable structure that lends significant insight into the workings of these hard-to-interpret models.

papers.title: FuxiTranyu: A Multilingual Large Language Model Trained with Balanced Data
papers.research_question: How to build a multilingual large language model with balanced data to mitigate performance discrepancies between high- and low-resource languages?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces FuxiTranyu, a multilingual LLM trained on balanced data, which shows competitive performance and more consistent multilingual representations compared to existing models.
papers.conclusion: FuxiTranyu is a strong open-source multilingual LLM, and balanced pre-training data is crucial for achieving consistent multilingual representations and performance.
papers.key_findings:
FuxiTranyu outperforms previous multilingual LLMs like BLOOM-7B1 and PolyLM-13B on several multilingual benchmarks.
Balanced pre-training data leads to more consistent multilingual representations across languages.
Neuron analysis reveals that deep layers are more language-specific and the importance of attention and MLP components varies across layers.
Languages with extremely limited resources (e.g., Bengali, Tamil) are allocated fewer neurons and perform poorly.
The model achieves high performance on summarization tasks, outperforming baseline models on XL-Sum.
papers.limitation:
Languages with extremely limited resources, such as Bengali and Tamil, are allocated with fewer neurons and perform poorly.
The model underperforms in some tasks (e.g., m-ARC, m-MMLU) due to limited training data for English.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated prowess in a wide range of tasks. However, many LLMs exhibit significant performance discrepancies between high- and low-resource languages. To mitigate this challenge, we present FuxiTranyu, an open-source multilingual LLM, which is designed to satisfy the need of the research community for balanced and high-performing multilingual capabilities. The base model, FuxiTranyu-8B, features 8 billion parameters and is trained from scratch on meticulously balanced multilingual data that contains 600 billion tokens covering 43 natural languages and 16 programming languages. We also develop two instruction-tuned models: FuxiTranyu-8B-SFT which is fine-tuned on a diverse multilingual instruction dataset, and FuxiTranyu-8B-DPO which is further refined with DPO on a preference dataset for enhanced alignment ability. Extensive experiments on a wide range of multilingual benchmarks demonstrate the competitive performance of FuxiTranyu against existing multilingual LLMs, e.g., BLOOM-7B, PolyLM-13B, and Mistral-7B-Instruct. Both neuron and representation interpretability analyses reveal that FuxiTranyu achieves consistent multilingual representations across languages. To promote further research into multilingual LLMs, we release both the base and instruction-tuned FuxiTranyu models together with 58 pre-training checkpoints at HuggingFace (see https://huggingface.co/TJUNLP/FuxiTranyu-8B) and Github (see https://github.com/tjunlp-lab/FuxiTranyu).

papers.title: On the Learning Mechanisms in Physical Reasoning
papers.research_question: Is dynamics prediction indispensable for physical reasoning? When performing physical reasoning, is it better for machines to learn from intuition by simply analyzing the static physical structure, or to learn from dynamics by predicting future states?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Learning from Intuition (LfI) can be as effective as Learning from Dynamics (LfD) for physical reasoning, and that LfD often degenerates to LfI due to inaccuracies in dynamics prediction, though accurate dynamics (ground truth) provide an upper bound.
papers.conclusion: LfI is a simpler and effective paradigm for physical reasoning, performing competitively with LfD, but the LfD route remains promising if dynamics prediction can be made significantly more accurate.
papers.key_findings:
Simple LfI models (e.g., ViT) achieve state-of-the-art performance on PHYRE-B, even outperforming LfD models in cross-template generalization.
Ground-truth dynamics significantly boost performance, indicating that dynamics can help if accurately predicted.
Approximate dynamics from predictors (e.g., PredRNN) do not improve over LfI and often cause the LfD pipeline to degenerate into LfI.
LfI models are design-efficient, require no extra object information, and generalize well to unseen scenarios.
The performance of LfI models can be further improved with better perceptual modules tailored for physical reasoning.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are conducted only on the PHYRE benchmark, lacking a rich suite of physical reasoning tasks.
LfI models are used without extra design for physical reasoning tasks, potentially leaving room for improvement.
The paper does not determine how accurate dynamics prediction needs to be to be beneficial.
future_direction: Develop a suite of physical reasoning tasks for further investigation.
Incorporate better perceptual modules and spatial analyzing modules into LfI models for physical reasoning.
Measure how accurate dynamics prediction needs to be to benefit downstream reasoning.
Explore how dynamics prediction can benefit other reasoning processes like counterfactual and hypothetical reasoning.
papers.abstract: Is dynamics prediction indispensable for physical reasoning? If so, what kind of roles do the dynamics prediction modules play during the physical reasoning process? Most studies focus on designing dynamics prediction networks and treating physical reasoning as a downstream task without investigating the questions above, taking for granted that the designed dynamics prediction would undoubtedly help the reasoning process. In this work, we take a closer look at this assumption, exploring this fundamental hypothesis by comparing two learning mechanisms: Learning from Dynamics (LfD) and Learning from Intuition (LfI). In the first experiment, we directly examine and compare these two mechanisms. Results show a surprising finding: Simple LfI is better than or on par with state-of-the-art LfD. This observation leads to the second experiment with Ground-truth Dynamics, the ideal case of LfD wherein dynamics are obtained directly from a simulator. Results show that dynamics, if directly given instead of approximated, would achieve much higher performance than LfI alone on physical reasoning; this essentially serves as the performance upper bound. Yet practically, LfD mechanism can only predict Approximate Dynamics using dynamics learning modules that mimic the physical laws, making the following downstream physical reasoning modules degenerate into the LfI paradigm; see the third experiment. We note that this issue is hard to mitigate, as dynamics prediction errors inevitably accumulate in the long horizon. Finally, in the fourth experiment, we note that LfI, the extremely simpler strategy when done right, is more effective in learning to solve physical reasoning problems. Taken together, the results on the challenging benchmark of PHYRE show that LfI is, if not better, as good as LfD for dynamics prediction. However, the potential improvement from LfD, though challenging, remains lucrative.

papers.title: Which Attention Heads Matter for In-Context Learning?
papers.research_question: Which attention heads (induction heads or function vector heads) are more important for in-context learning in transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: Function vector (FV) heads are the primary drivers of few-shot in-context learning performance, especially in larger models, and many FV heads evolve from induction heads during training.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that function vector heads are crucial for in-context learning, challenging the prevailing view that induction heads are the key mechanism, and highlights methodological insights for interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
FV heads are more important for few-shot ICL than induction heads, especially in larger models.
Induction heads and FV heads are distinct but correlated.
Many FV heads start as induction heads during training and then transition to the FV mechanism.
The choice of metric (few-shot accuracy vs. token-loss difference) leads to different conclusions about the importance of induction heads.
The relative importance of FV heads increases with model scale.
future_direction: Investigate why induction heads might be necessary precursors to FV heads.
Determine the role of remaining induction heads in fully trained models.
Explore additional mechanisms that could explain ICL capabilities.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive in-context learning (ICL) capability, enabling them to perform new tasks using only a few demonstrations in the prompt. Two different mechanisms have been proposed to explain ICL: induction heads that find and copy relevant tokens, and function vector (FV) heads whose activations compute a latent encoding of the ICL task. To better understand which of the two distinct mechanisms drives ICL, we study and compare induction heads and FV heads in 12 language models. Through detailed ablations, we discover that few-shot ICL performance depends primarily on FV heads, especially in larger models. In addition, we uncover that FV and induction heads are connected: many FV heads start as induction heads during training before transitioning to the FV mechanism. This leads us to speculate that induction facilitates learning the more complex FV mechanism that ultimately drives ICL.

papers.title: A Differential Manifold Perspective and Universality Analysis of Continuous Attractors in Artificial Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we establish a unified mathematical framework to analyze continuous attractors in artificial neural networks from a differential manifold perspective?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a unified framework based on differential manifolds and Jacobian matrix analysis to study continuous attractors, demonstrating universal singular value stratification in classification networks and linking attractor dimensionality to eigenvalue/singular value structure.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a novel, unified approach to investigating continuous attractors via eigenvalue/singular value analysis of the Jacobian, validates the prevalence of stratification in classification networks, and lays a foundation for a general theory of attractors in neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed differential manifold framework is compatible with prior conclusions about continuous attractors.
Continuous attractor phenomena are linked to eigenvalues of the local Jacobian matrix, with stratification indicating approximate attractor behavior.
Singular value stratification is universal across common classification models (MLP, CNN, ResNet) and datasets (MNIST, CIFAR-10, Fruit).
The framework can determine the dimensionality of continuous attractors via the rank of the Jacobian.
Approximate continuous attractor behavior, indicated by eigenvalue/singular value stratification, emerges during neural network training and correlates with generalization.
papers.limitation:
Lacks a rigorous mathematical derivation extending eigenvalue stratification to singular value stratification.
The existence of continuous attractors in tasks beyond classification remains an open question.
future_direction: Develop a general theory of continuous attractors in neural networks.
Apply the methodology to deep neural networks to study optimization landscapes, generalization mechanisms, and training stability.
papers.abstract: Continuous attractors are critical for information processing in both biological and artificial neural systems, with implications for spatial navigation, memory, and deep learning optimization. However, existing research lacks a unified framework to analyze their properties across diverse dynamical systems, limiting cross-architectural generalizability. This study establishes a novel framework from the perspective of differential manifolds to investigate continuous attractors in artificial neural networks. It verifies compatibility with prior conclusions, elucidates links between continuous attractor phenomena and eigenvalues of the local Jacobian matrix, and demonstrates the universality of singular value stratification in common classification models and datasets. These findings suggest continuous attractors may be ubiquitous in general neural networks, highlighting the need for a general theory, with the proposed framework offering a promising foundation given the close mathematical connection between eigenvalues and singular values.

papers.title: Dynamical Tests of a Deep Learning Weather Prediction Model
papers.abstract: Abstract Global deep learning weather prediction models have recently been shown to produce forecasts that rival those from physics-based models run at operational centers. It is unclear whether these models have encoded atmospheric dynamics or simply pattern matching that produces the smallest forecast error. Answering this question is crucial to establishing the utility of these models as tools for basic science. Here, we subject one such model, Pangu-Weather, to a set of four classical dynamical experiments that do not resemble the model training data. Localized perturbations to the model output and the initial conditions are added to steady time-averaged conditions, to assess the propagation speed and structural evolution of signals away from the local source. Perturbing the model physics by adding a steady tropical heat source results in a classical Matsuno–Gill response near the heating and planetary waves that radiate into the extratropics. A localized disturbance on the winter-averaged North Pacific jet stream produces realistic extratropical cyclones and fronts, including the spontaneous emergence of polar lows. Perturbing the 500-hPa height field alone yields adjustment from a state of rest to one of wind–pressure balance over ∼6 h. Localized subtropical low pressure systems produce Atlantic hurricanes, provided the initial amplitude exceeds about 4 hPa, and setting the initial humidity to zero eliminates hurricane development. We conclude that the model encodes realistic physics in all experiments and suggest that it can be used as a tool for rapidly testing a wide range of hypotheses.

papers.title: Toward Data‐Driven Weather and Climate Forecasting: Approximating a Simple General Circulation Model With Deep Learning
papers.abstract: Abstract It is shown that it is possible to emulate the dynamics of a simple general circulation model with a deep neural network. After being trained on the model, the network can predict the complete model state several time steps ahead—which conceptually is making weather forecasts in the model world. Additionally, after being initialized with an arbitrary model state, the network can through repeatedly feeding back its predictions into its inputs create a climate run, which has similar climate statistics to the climate of the general circulation model. This network climate run shows no long‐term drift, even though no conservation properties were explicitly designed into the network.

papers.title: M‐ENIAC: A Physics‐Informed Machine Learning Recreation of the First Successful Numerical Weather Forecasts
papers.abstract: Abstract In 1950 the first successful numerical weather forecast was obtained by solving the barotropic vorticity equation using the Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer (ENIAC), which marked the beginning of the age of numerical weather prediction. Here, we ask the question of how these numerical forecasts would have turned out, if machine learning based solvers had been used instead of standard numerical discretizations. Specifically, we recreate these numerical forecasts using physics‐informed neural networks. We show that physics‐informed neural networks provide an easier and more accurate methodology for solving meteorological equations on the sphere, as compared to the ENIAC solver.

papers.title: Physics-Assisted and Topology-Informed Deep Learning for Weather Prediction
papers.abstract: Although deep learning models have demonstrated remarkable potential in weather prediction, most of them overlook either the \textbf{physics} of the underlying weather evolution or the \textbf{topology} of the Earth's surface. In light of these disadvantages, we develop PASSAT, a novel Physics-ASSisted And Topology-informed deep learning model for weather prediction. PASSAT attributes the weather evolution to two key factors: (i) the advection process that can be characterized by the advection equation and the Navier-Stokes equation; (ii) the Earth-atmosphere interaction that is difficult to both model and calculate. PASSAT also takes the topology of the Earth's surface into consideration, other than simply treating it as a plane. With these considerations, PASSAT numerically solves the advection equation and the Navier-Stokes equation on the spherical manifold, utilizes a spherical graph neural network to capture the Earth-atmosphere interaction, and generates the initial velocity fields that are critical to solving the advection equation from the same spherical graph neural network. In the $5.625^\circ$-resolution ERA5 data set, PASSAT outperforms both the state-of-the-art deep learning-based weather prediction models and the operational numerical weather prediction model IFS T42. Code and checkpoint are available at https://github.com/Yumenomae/PASSAT_5p625.

papers.title: Challenges of learning multi-scale dynamics with AI weather models: Implications for stability and one solution
papers.abstract: Long-term stability and physical consistency are critical properties for AI-based weather models if they are going to be used for subseasonal-to-seasonal forecasts or beyond, e.g., climate change projection. However, current AI-based weather models can only provide short-term forecasts accurately since they become unstable or physically inconsistent when time-integrated beyond a few weeks or a few months. Either they exhibit numerical blow-up or hallucinate unrealistic dynamics of the atmospheric variables, akin to the current class of autoregressive large language models. The cause of the instabilities is unknown, and the methods that are used to improve their stability horizons are ad-hoc and lack rigorous theory. In this paper, we reveal that the universal causal mechanism for these instabilities in any turbulent flow is due to \textit{spectral bias} wherein, \textit{any} deep learning architecture is biased to learn only the large-scale dynamics and ignores the small scales completely. We further elucidate how turbulence physics and the absence of convergence in deep learning-based time-integrators amplify this bias, leading to unstable error propagation. Finally, using the quasi-geostrophic flow and European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasting (ECMWF) Reanalysis data as test cases, we bridge the gap between deep learning theory and numerical analysis to propose one mitigative solution to such unphysical behavior. We develop long-term physically-consistent data-driven models for the climate system and demonstrate accurate short-term forecasts, and hundreds of years of time-integration with accurate mean and variability.

papers.title: Interpreting and Stabilizing Machine-Learning Parametrizations of Convection
papers.abstract: Abstract Neural networks are a promising technique for parameterizing subgrid-scale physics (e.g., moist atmospheric convection) in coarse-resolution climate models, but their lack of interpretability and reliability prevents widespread adoption. For instance, it is not fully understood why neural network parameterizations often cause dramatic instability when coupled to atmospheric fluid dynamics. This paper introduces tools for interpreting their behavior that are customized to the parameterization task. First, we assess the nonlinear sensitivity of a neural network to lower-tropospheric stability and the midtropospheric moisture, two widely studied controls of moist convection. Second, we couple the linearized response functions of these neural networks to simplified gravity wave dynamics, and analytically diagnose the corresponding phase speeds, growth rates, wavelengths, and spatial structures. To demonstrate their versatility, these techniques are tested on two sets of neural networks, one trained with a superparameterized version of the Community Atmosphere Model (SPCAM) and the second with a near-global cloud-resolving model (GCRM). Even though the SPCAM simulation has a warmer climate than the cloud-resolving model, both neural networks predict stronger heating/drying in moist and unstable environments, which is consistent with observations.
