In contrast, AI systems often fail to extract consistent physical rules from video, relying on black-box mechanisms that produce implausible outcomes. We introduce the Intuitive World Model (IWM), designed to learn physical principles directly from vision, mimicking human intuition. Drawing inspiration from developmental psychology, IWM utilizes a modular architecture to decompose interactions into force-based dynamics. Through observing objects collide and interact via charges, it identifies intrinsic properties like mass and charge and learns representations analogous to Newton's and Coulomb's laws. This paradigm uniquely allows neural networks to provide explicit explanations for physical phenomena and conduct counterfactual reasoning consistent with learned physical laws. Our work demonstrates that a developmentally-inspired approach empowers AI to acquire explicit, interpretable physical knowledge from observation, mirroring a core aspect of human intelligence.

papers.title: Predictive learning as a network mechanism for extracting low-dimensional latent space representations
papers.research_question: Does learning to predict future observations cause neural networks to extract low-dimensional latent structure from their sensory inputs?
papers.core_contribution: Predictive learning in neural networks leads to the emergence of low-dimensional internal representations that linearly encode the latent variables of the environment, a process that can be quantified using novel metrics like latent signal transfer and dimensionality gain.
papers.conclusion: Predictive learning is a network mechanism for extracting low-dimensional latent space representations from high-dimensional sensory inputs, which can be characterized by the introduced metrics and analytical tools.
papers.key_findings:
Predictive learning causes neural networks to form low-dimensional representations that map the latent structure of the sensory environment.
Latent space signal transfer occurs during learning, where latent variables become increasingly linearly decodable from the top principal components of the neural representation.
Dimensionality gain (the ratio of linear to nonlinear dimensionality) increases during predictive learning, indicating the extraction of a low-dimensional manifold from high-dimensional observations.
Predictive learning leads to the emergence of neurons with localized activations on the manifold (manifold cells).
Representations formed by predictive learning are more structured and better reflect the latent space than those formed by autoencoding (non-predictive learning).
future_direction: Further testing of the predictive learning framework in neural data.
Application of the framework to additional tasks beyond spatial exploration and arm-reaching.
Investigation of predictive learning as a general principle for representation formation in both biological and artificial neural networks.
papers.abstract: Artificial neural networks have recently achieved many successes in solving sequential processing and planning tasks. Their success is often ascribed to the emergence of the task's low-dimensional latent structure in the network activity - i.e., in the learned neural representations. Here, we investigate the hypothesis that a means for generating representations with easily accessed low-dimensional latent structure, possibly reflecting an underlying semantic organization, is through learning to predict observations about the world. Specifically, we ask whether and when network mechanisms for sensory prediction coincide with those for extracting the underlying latent variables. Using a recurrent neural network model trained to predict a sequence of observations we show that network dynamics exhibit low-dimensional but nonlinearly transformed representations of sensory inputs that map the latent structure of the sensory environment. We quantify these results using nonlinear measures of intrinsic dimensionality and linear decodability of latent variables, and provide mathematical arguments for why such useful predictive representations emerge. We focus throughout on how our results can aid the analysis and interpretation of experimental data.

papers.title: LLM Circuit Analyses Are Consistent Across Training and Scale
papers.research_question: Do circuit analyses of LLMs generalize across training time and model scale?
papers.core_contribution: Circuit analyses are consistent across training and scale: task abilities and supporting functional components emerge at similar token counts across model sizes, and the overarching algorithms implemented by circuits remain stable even when individual components change.
papers.conclusion: Circuit analyses generalize well over both training and scale, suggesting that studies on small models at the end of pre-training can inform understanding of larger models and models with longer training.
papers.key_findings:
Task abilities and functional components (e.g., induction heads, name-mover heads) emerge consistently at similar token counts across different model scales.
The algorithm implemented by a circuit remains stable over training even when the specific attention heads implementing it change.
Circuit size correlates with model size and can fluctuate over time while the algorithm remains the same.
Components like induction heads emerge around 2B tokens across scales, paralleling task learning curves.
Circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training provide insights that generalize to larger models and longer training runs.
papers.limitation:
The study does not include fine-tuning or other post-training techniques.
Circuit completeness is challenging to verify.
The findings need validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
future_direction: Validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
Investigating the load-balancing mechanism that maintains task performance when components change.
papers.abstract: Most currently deployed large language models (LLMs) undergo continuous training or additional finetuning. By contrast, most research into LLMs' internal mechanisms focuses on models at one snapshot in time (the end of pre-training), raising the question of whether their results generalize to real-world settings. Existing studies of mechanisms over time focus on encoder-only or toy models, which differ significantly from most deployed models. In this study, we track how model mechanisms, operationalized as circuits, emerge and evolve across 300 billion tokens of training in decoder-only LLMs, in models ranging from 70 million to 2.8 billion parameters. We find that task abilities and the functional components that support them emerge consistently at similar token counts across scale. Moreover, although such components may be implemented by different attention heads over time, the overarching algorithm that they implement remains. Surprisingly, both these algorithms and the types of components involved therein can replicate across model scale. These results suggest that circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training can provide insights that still apply after additional pre-training and over model scale.

papers.title: Ensuring Medical AI Safety: Interpretability-Driven Detection and Mitigation of Spurious Model Behavior and Associated Data
papers.research_question: How can interpretability methods be used to detect and mitigate spurious correlations (shortcut learning) in deep neural networks for medical AI, and how can bias annotation be semi-automated to reduce manual labeling effort?
papers.core_contribution: The paper extends the Reveal2Revise framework with semi-automated interpretability-based bias annotation capabilities, enabling sample- and feature-level annotation of spurious correlations to reduce manual labeling and improve bias mitigation in medical AI models.
papers.conclusion: The interpretability-driven Reveal2Revise framework, enhanced with bias annotation capabilities, provides a comprehensive approach to improve medical AI safety by detecting and mitigating spurious model behavior, ultimately increasing model robustness for real-world deployment.
papers.key_findings:
The extended Reveal2Revise framework successfully identifies and mitigates both controlled and real-world spurious correlations across four medical datasets and multiple model architectures.
The framework provides sample-level bias annotation via data retrieval using concept representations (e.g., CAVs) and feature-level annotation via spatial localization of artifacts.
Bias mitigation methods like RRR and RR-ClArC, when integrated with the framework, improve model robustness by reducing reliance on spurious features while maintaining accuracy on clean data.
The approach reduces the need for extensive manual annotation by domain experts, making bias detection and mitigation more practical.
The framework is applicable across different modalities (image and ECG) and model types (CNNs and Vision Transformers).
papers.limitation:
The framework requires human validation to distinguish between clinically valid and spurious outlier behavior.
Some artifacts are non-localizable (e.g., brightness shifts), limiting spatial bias localization.
Bias representations (e.g., CAVs) may be inaccurate if the initial set of biased samples is small or noisy.
future_direction: Extending the framework to other modalities and data types.
Improving the automation of bias detection and validation to further reduce human effort.
Integrating the framework with a wider range of bias mitigation techniques.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are increasingly employed in high-stakes medical applications, despite their tendency for shortcut learning in the presence of spurious correlations, which can have potentially fatal consequences in practice. Whereas a multitude of works address either the detection or mitigation of such shortcut behavior in isolation, the Reveal2Revise approach provides a comprehensive bias mitigation framework combining these steps. However, effectively addressing these biases often requires substantial labeling efforts from domain experts. In this work, we review the steps of the Reveal2Revise framework and enhance it with semi-automated interpretability-based bias annotation capabilities. This includes methods for the sample- and feature-level bias annotation, providing valuable information for bias mitigation methods to unlearn the undesired shortcut behavior. We show the applicability of the framework using four medical datasets across two modalities, featuring controlled and real-world spurious correlations caused by data artifacts. We successfully identify and mitigate these biases in VGG16, ResNet50, and contemporary Vision Transformer models, ultimately increasing their robustness and applicability for real-world medical tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/frederikpahde/medical-ai-safety.

papers.title: Using Degeneracy in the Loss Landscape for Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How does degeneracy in neural network parameterizations obfuscate internal structure for mechanistic interpretability, and how can we remove these degeneracies to obtain more interpretable representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the concept of degeneracy in neural network parameterizations as an obstacle to interpretability, characterizes three sources of degeneracy, and proposes the Interaction Basis, a technique to obtain a representation invariant to these degeneracies, which may lead to sparser and more interpretable representations.
papers.conclusion: The paper argues that degeneracy in neural network parameterizations hinders interpretability, identifies sources of degeneracy, and proposes the Interaction Basis to remove degeneracies, potentially yielding sparser and more interpretable representations.
papers.key_findings:
Neural network parameters can be degenerate due to linear dependence between activations in a layer, linear dependence between gradients passed back to a layer, and ReLUs which fire on the same subset of datapoints.
Modular networks are likely to be more degenerate, and a metric for identifying modules is developed based on this argument.
The Interaction Basis is a tractable technique to obtain a representation invariant to degeneracies from linear dependence of activations or Jacobians.
Representations invariant to degeneracies are likely to have sparser interactions.
The effective parameter count, derived from the local learning coefficient, measures the number of computationally relevant parameters in the network.
papers.limitation: The derivation of the Interaction Basis relies on two simplifying assumptions of independence about the Hessian, which are strong assumptions.
future_direction: Investigate alternative techniques for finding a basis without the simplifying assumptions about the Hessian.
Determine how to choose an appropriate behavioral loss cutoff epsilon for finite data singular learning theory.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability aims to reverse engineer the algorithms implemented by neural networks by studying their weights and activations. An obstacle to reverse engineering neural networks is that many of the parameters inside a network are not involved in the computation being implemented by the network. These degenerate parameters may obfuscate internal structure. Singular learning theory teaches us that neural network parameterizations are biased towards being more degenerate, and parameterizations with more degeneracy are likely to generalize further. We identify 3 ways that network parameters can be degenerate: linear dependence between activations in a layer; linear dependence between gradients passed back to a layer; ReLUs which fire on the same subset of datapoints. We also present a heuristic argument that modular networks are likely to be more degenerate, and we develop a metric for identifying modules in a network that is based on this argument. We propose that if we can represent a neural network in a way that is invariant to reparameterizations that exploit the degeneracies, then this representation is likely to be more interpretable, and we provide some evidence that such a representation is likely to have sparser interactions. We introduce the Interaction Basis, a tractable technique to obtain a representation that is invariant to degeneracies from linear dependence of activations or Jacobians.

papers.title: A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits
papers.research_question: How can we reverse engineer the internal computations of transformer language models using a mathematical framework?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a mathematical framework for understanding transformer circuits, enabling reverse engineering of small attention-only models and identifying induction heads as key for in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: The mathematical framework provides a foundation for understanding transformer circuits, with induction heads as a critical component for in-context learning, paving the way for future work on larger models.
papers.key_findings:
Zero-layer transformers model bigram statistics, accessible directly from weights.
One-layer attention-only transformers are ensembles of bigram and skip-trigram models, enabling simple in-context learning.
Two-layer attention-only transformers implement induction heads through attention head composition, allowing more complex in-context learning.
Induction heads use a sophisticated algorithm to repeat previous sequences based on token similarity.
The framework allows direct analysis of weight matrices to understand model behavior without running the model.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on attention-only transformers, excluding MLP layers which are harder to interpret.
Preliminary and not applied to larger, more complex models.
future_direction: Apply the framework to larger and more realistic models.
Investigate MLP layers in transformers.
papers.abstract: How can we reverse engineer the internal computations of transformer language models using a mathematical framework? Introduces a mathematical framework for understanding transformer circuits, enabling reverse engineering of small attention-only models and identifying induction heads as key for in-context learning. The mathematical framework provides a foundation for understanding transformer circuits, with induction heads as a critical component for in-context learning, paving the way for future work on larger models.

papers.title: Scaling Laws and Interpretability of Learning from Repeated Data
papers.research_question: What are the effects of repeated data on language model training, and how does it mechanistically affect model components like induction heads?
papers.core_contribution: Repeated data causes a double-descent phenomenon in language models, leading to severe performance degradation that is mechanistically linked to disproportionate damage to induction heads and copying mechanisms, shifting the model from generalization to memorization.
papers.conclusion: Small fractions of repeated data, if repeated at a specific frequency, can cause surprisingly severe performance degradation in language models, and this degradation is associated with disproportionate damage to internal mechanisms like induction heads that support generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Repeated data induces a strong double-descent phenomenon, with a predictable range of repetition frequency causing severe performance degradation.
A small fraction of repeated data (e.g., 0.1% repeated 100 times) can degrade an 800M parameter model's performance to that of a 400M parameter model.
Repeated data disproportionately damages copying ability and induction heads, which are internal structures associated with generalization.
The damage to induction heads provides a mechanistic explanation for the shift from generalization to memorization.
The double-descent phenomenon and associated performance degradation are also observed when training on Python code data.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have been trained on vast datasets, but also often on repeated data, either intentionally for the purpose of upweighting higher quality data, or unintentionally because data deduplication is not perfect and the model is exposed to repeated data at the sentence, paragraph, or document level. Some works have reported substantial negative performance effects of this repeated data. In this paper we attempt to study repeated data systematically and to understand its effects mechanistically. To do this, we train a family of models where most of the data is unique but a small fraction of it is repeated many times. We find a strong double descent phenomenon, in which repeated data can lead test loss to increase midway through training. A predictable range of repetition frequency leads to surprisingly severe degradation in performance. For instance, performance of an 800M parameter model can be degraded to that of a 2x smaller model (400M params) by repeating 0.1% of the data 100 times, despite the other 90% of the training tokens remaining unique. We suspect there is a range in the middle where the data can be memorized and doing so consumes a large fraction of the model's capacity, and this may be where the peak of degradation occurs. Finally, we connect these observations to recent mechanistic interpretability work - attempting to reverse engineer the detailed computations performed by the model - by showing that data repetition disproportionately damages copying and internal structures associated with generalization, such as induction heads, providing a possible mechanism for the shift from generalization to memorization. Taken together, these results provide a hypothesis for why repeating a relatively small fraction of data in large language models could lead to disproportionately large harms to performance.

papers.title: Induction Heads as an Essential Mechanism for Pattern Matching in In-context Learning
papers.research_question: What is the role of induction heads in few-shot in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides empirical evidence that induction heads, through their prefix matching and copying mechanism, are a fundamental component enabling few-shot in-context learning in large language models.
papers.conclusion: Induction heads are a fundamental mechanism underlying in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
Ablating a small percentage (1-3%) of induction heads leads to substantial decreases in ICL performance, much more so than ablating random heads.
Blocking the specific induction attention pattern (via attention knockout) causes performance drops similar to full head ablation, confirming the mechanism's specific role.
The importance of induction heads for ICL holds across abstract pattern recognition tasks and real-world NLP tasks.
Induction heads utilize a 'fuzzy' version of the prefix matching and copying mechanism to enable pattern matching in ICL.
The ablation of induction heads affects few-shot performance more severely than zero-shot performance, highlighting their role in learning from examples.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on prefix-matching scores as a proxy for identifying induction heads, lacking a mechanistic basis for definitive identification.
Attention knockout experiments are confined to abstract-pattern recognition tasks; further research is required for NLP tasks.
The experiments do not test whether induction heads are the only computational process contributing to ICL; other mechanisms may exist.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown a remarkable ability to learn and perform complex tasks through in-context learning (ICL). However, a comprehensive understanding of its internal mechanisms is still lacking. This paper explores the role of induction heads in a few-shot ICL setting. We analyse two state-of-the-art models, Llama-3-8B and InternLM2-20B on abstract pattern recognition and NLP tasks. Our results show that even a minimal ablation of induction heads leads to ICL performance decreases of up to ~32% for abstract pattern recognition tasks, bringing the performance close to random. For NLP tasks, this ablation substantially decreases the model's ability to benefit from examples, bringing few-shot ICL performance close to that of zero-shot prompts. We further use attention knockout to disable specific induction patterns, and present fine-grained evidence for the role that the induction mechanism plays in ICL.

papers.title: Deconstructing Recurrence, Attention, and Gating: Investigating the transferability of Transformers and Gated Recurrent Neural Networks in forecasting of dynamical systems
papers.research_question: What are the key architectural components (gating, attention, recurrence) that enable forecasting accuracy in Transformers and RNNs, and how can they be combined to improve performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that neural gating and attention improve RNNs, while recurrence harms Transformers, and that a hybrid architecture combining Recurrent Highway Networks with gating and attention performs best for spatiotemporal forecasting.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that core mechanisms like gating, attention, and recurrence should be treated as hyperparameters and tuned for each task, leading to improved forecasting performance, with the best architecture being a hybrid Recurrent Highway Network with gating and attention.
papers.key_findings:
Neural gating and attention improve the performance of standard RNNs in most forecasting tasks.
Adding recurrence to Transformers is detrimental to their forecasting performance.
A hybrid architecture integrating Recurrent Highway Networks with neural gating and attention mechanisms emerges as the best performing model for high-dimensional spatiotemporal forecasting.
Transformers train faster than RNNs but RNNs achieve higher forecasting accuracy.
The effectiveness of gating mechanisms (coupled vs. uncoupled) is task-dependent.
papers.abstract: Machine learning architectures, including transformers and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have revolutionized forecasting in applications ranging from text processing to extreme weather. Notably, advanced network architectures, tuned for applications such as natural language processing, are transferable to other tasks such as spatiotemporal forecasting tasks. However, there is a scarcity of ablation studies to illustrate the key components that enable this forecasting accuracy. The absence of such studies, although explainable due to the associated computational cost, intensifies the belief that these models ought to be considered as black boxes. In this work, we decompose the key architectural components of the most powerful neural architectures, namely gating and recurrence in RNNs, and attention mechanisms in transformers. Then, we synthesize and build novel hybrid architectures from the standard blocks, performing ablation studies to identify which mechanisms are effective for each task. The importance of considering these components as hyper-parameters that can augment the standard architectures is exhibited on various forecasting datasets, from the spatiotemporal chaotic dynamics of the multiscale Lorenz 96 system, the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation, as well as standard real world time-series benchmarks. A key finding is that neural gating and attention improves the performance of all standard RNNs in most tasks, while the addition of a notion of recurrence in transformers is detrimental. Furthermore, our study reveals that a novel, sparsely used, architecture which integrates Recurrent Highway Networks with neural gating and attention mechanisms, emerges as the best performing architecture in high-dimensional spatiotemporal forecasting of dynamical systems.

papers.title: Neural Earthquake Forecasting with Minimal Information: Limits, Interpretability, and the Role of Markov Structure
papers.research_question: Can neural and hybrid models for earthquake forecasting generalize temporally when trained on early data and tested on future unseen events?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a hybrid neural-Markov model for earthquake forecasting and a temporal cross-validation framework, showing that model performance degrades on future data due to non-stationarity, highlighting the importance of temporal evaluation.
papers.conclusion: Neural and hybrid models for earthquake forecasting fail to generalize to future data due to temporal non-stationarity, highlighting the need for temporally realistic evaluation and caution in applying machine learning to sparse forecasting settings.
papers.key_findings:
The hybrid model outperforms the Markov baseline on validation data but fails to generalize to the most recent quintile of the catalog.
The final quintile of seismicity exhibits more Markov-consistent behavior than earlier data, indicating temporal non-stationarity.
Integrated Gradients attribution shows a shift in feature importance between validation and test sets, with magnitude features becoming more relevant in the test set.
Temporal cross-validation reveals that model performance is highly dependent on the temporal location of the test data, with the last quintile consistently underperforming.
The study underscores the risk of overfitting to early patterns and the need for temporally realistic benchmarks in earthquake forecasting.
papers.limitation:
Small sample size affects all statistical models based on this data.
Sparse input features limited to simple descriptors of past events restrict the models' ability to capture complex physical dynamics.
The Markov prior is static and unable to account for possible changes in seismic regimes.
Results are based on a single regional earthquake catalog without additional geophysical or contextual data.
Only feedforward architectures were considered; models with more explicit temporal reasoning were not explored.
future_direction: Refine the use of prior knowledge with dynamic extensions of the Markov model or hierarchical priors that adapt across segments of the catalog.
Incorporate additional physical variables such as fault-specific information, geodetic signals, or stress evolution proxies.
Explore dynamically updated models or time-aware architectures to track evolving patterns more effectively.
papers.abstract: Abstract Forecasting earthquake sequences remains a central challenge in seismology, particularly under non-stationary conditions. While deep learning models have shown promise, their ability to generalize across time remains poorly understood. We evaluate neural and hybrid (NN + Markov) models for short-term earthquake forecasting on a regional catalog using temporally stratified cross-validation. Models are trained on earlier portions of the catalog and evaluated on future unseen events, enabling realistic assessment of temporal generalization. We find that while these models outperform a purely Markovian model on validation data, their test performance degrades substantially in the most recent quintile. A detailed attribution analysis reveals a shift in feature relevance over time, with later data exhibiting simpler, more Markov-consistent behavior. To support interpretability, we apply Integrated Gradients, a type of explainable AI (XAI) to analyze how models rely on different input features. These results highlight the risks of overfitting to early patterns in seismicity and underscore the importance of temporally realistic benchmarks. We conclude that forecasting skill is inherently time-dependent and benefits from combining physical priors with data-driven methods.

papers.title: Unveiling the Mystery of Weight in Large Foundation Models: Gaussian Distribution Never Fades
papers.research_question: What are the distributional properties of weights in large foundation models, and how can these properties be leveraged to simplify model adaptation and editing?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that weights in large foundation models follow a Gaussian distribution and that transformation weights can be derived from Gaussian noise, leading to a method that improves adaptation and editing by adjusting the standard deviation of the noise and updating outliers.
papers.conclusion: The Gaussian distribution of weights is a fundamental property that can be leveraged to simplify adaptation and editing, and optimal weights are sparse with a Gaussian-like distribution.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-trained weights of LFMs predominantly follow a Gaussian distribution.
Transformation weights (∆W) can be derived from Gaussian noise and primarily increase the standard deviation of pre-trained weights.
The standard deviation of transformation weights grows with layer depth.
Optimal weights should exhibit zero-mean, symmetry, and sparsity, with sparse values following a truncated Gaussian distribution and a few outliers.
Adaptation and editing can be improved by adjusting Gaussian signals and outliers.
papers.abstract: This paper presents a pioneering exploration of the mechanisms underlying large foundation models' (LFMs) weights, aiming to simplify AI research. Through extensive observation and analysis on prevailing LFMs, we find that regardless of initialization strategies, their weights predominantly follow a Gaussian distribution, with occasional sharp, inverted T-shaped, or linear patterns. We further discover that the weights share the i.i.d. properties of Gaussian noise, and explore their direct relationship. We find that transformation weights can be derived from Gaussian noise, and they primarily serve to increase the standard deviation of pre-trained weights, with their standard deviation growing with layer depth. In other words, transformation weights broaden the acceptable deviation from the optimal weights, facilitating adaptation to downstream tasks. Building upon the above conclusions, we thoroughly discussed the nature of optimal weights, ultimately concluding that they should exhibit zero-mean, symmetry, and sparsity, with the sparse values being a truncated Gaussian distribution and a few outliers. Our experiments in LFM adaptation and editing demonstrate the effectiveness of these insights. We hope these findings can provide a foundational understanding to pave the way for future advancements in the LFM community.

papers.title: How 'Neural' is a Neural Foundation Model?
papers.research_question: Do neural decoding and encoding manifolds reveal new insights into how foundation models represent temporal response patterns? Are their representations brain-like?
papers.core_contribution: The recurrent module of the neural foundation model shows brain-like representational properties, while the feedforward encoder and readout module have limitations; design changes are suggested for better biological alignment.
papers.conclusion: The FNN is only a partial digital twin of the mouse visual system; its recurrent module is most brain-like, but design improvements in early recurrence and readout constraints could enhance biological alignment.
papers.key_findings:
The recurrent module achieves the highest stimulus separability and closest alignment with biological visual cortex.
The feedforward encoder lacks biologically plausible temporal patterns and contains non-selective neurons.
The readout module uses numerous specialized feature maps rather than biologically plausible mechanisms.
Decoding trajectories in the recurrent stage show tubular structure but fewer crossings than biological data, indicating less complex dynamics.
Encoding manifolds reveal that the FNN's neuronal organization, especially in the readout, is clustered by feature maps and differs from the continuous topology of biological cortex.
papers.limitation:
The FNN does not fully capture the complexity of neural dynamics, as evidenced by fewer crossings in decoding trajectories compared to biological data.
The readout module's highly clustered, feature-map-based organization is not brain-like.
future_direction: Introduce recurrence in early encoder stages.
Constraining features in the readout module to be more biologically plausible.
Investigate more complex temporal processing to better match biological dynamics.
papers.abstract: Foundation models have shown remarkable success in fitting biological visual systems; however, their black-box nature inherently limits their utility for understanding brain function. Here, we peek inside a SOTA foundation model of neural activity (Wang et al., 2025) as a physiologist might, characterizing each 'neuron' based on its temporal response properties to parametric stimuli. We analyze how different stimuli are represented in neural activity space by building decoding manifolds, and we analyze how different neurons are represented in stimulus-response space by building neural encoding manifolds. We find that the different processing stages of the model (i.e., the feedforward encoder, recurrent, and readout modules) each exhibit qualitatively different representational structures in these manifolds. The recurrent module shows a jump in capabilities over the encoder module by 'pushing apart' the representations of different temporal stimulus patterns. Our 'tubularity' metric quantifies this stimulus-dependent development of neural activity as biologically plausible. The readout module achieves high fidelity by using numerous specialized feature maps rather than biologically plausible mechanisms. Overall, this study provides a window into the inner workings of a prominent neural foundation model, gaining insights into the biological relevance of its internals through the novel analysis of its neurons' joint temporal response patterns. Our findings suggest design changes that could bring neural foundation models into closer alignment with biological systems: introducing recurrence in early encoder stages, and constraining features in the readout module.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability as Statistical Estimation: A Variance Analysis
papers.research_question: What is the stability of mechanistic interpretability methods, specifically circuit discovery, and how does variance in causal mediation analysis and its approximations affect the reliability of discovered circuits?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that circuit discovery methods are highly unstable due to intrinsic variance in causal mediation analysis scores and amplification by approximation methods, advocating for more rigorous statistical practices in mechanistic interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Circuit discovery is not a stable process and requires statistical rigor, including reporting stability metrics and sensitivity analyses, to become a reliable scientific tool.
papers.key_findings:
Exact causal mediation analysis (CMA) scores exhibit high intrinsic variance across inputs, meaning the causal effect of a component is a volatile random variable.
Approximation methods like Edge Attribution Patching (EAP) amplify this variance, leading to low signal-to-noise ratios.
Circuit discovery pipelines are sensitive to data resampling, hyperparameters, and counterfactual definitions, resulting in structurally inconsistent circuits.
Larger models (e.g., Llama-3.2-1B) show higher variability in circuit discovery compared to smaller models (e.g., gpt2-small).
The instability of circuits is not mitigated by instruction tuning (comparing Llama-3.2-1B and its instruct variant).
papers.limitation:
Focus on the EAP family of methods, leaving out newer methods that may have different properties.
Exact CMA analysis was only done on gpt2-small for the IOI task due to computational constraints.
Limited to three classic MI tasks, which may not generalize to fuzzier reasoning tasks.
Stability metrics treat all edges equally, whereas weighted metrics might reveal a stable functional core.
future_direction: Probabilistic circuit discovery: characterizing a distribution over possible circuits.
Decomposing variance into estimator variance and intrinsic variance.
Stability-aware optimization: developing objectives that explicitly optimize for stability.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) aims to reverse-engineer model behaviors by identifying functional sub-networks. Yet, the scientific validity of these findings depends on their stability. In this work, we argue that circuit discovery is not a standalone task but a statistical estimation problem built upon causal mediation analysis (CMA). We uncover a fundamental instability at this base layer: exact, single-input CMA scores exhibit high intrinsic variance, implying that the causal effect of a component is a volatile random variable rather than a fixed property. We then demonstrate that circuit discovery pipelines inherit this variance and further amplify it. Fast approximation methods, such as Edge Attribution Patching and its successors, introduce additional estimation noise, while aggregating these noisy scores over datasets leads to fragile structural estimates. Consequently, small perturbations in input data or hyperparameters yield vastly different circuits. We systematically decompose these sources of variance and advocate for more rigorous MI practices, prioritizing statistical robustness and routine reporting of stability metrics.

papers.title: Video Prediction of Dynamic Physical Simulations With Pixel-Space Spatiotemporal Transformers
papers.research_question: This study investigates a transformer adaptation for video prediction with a simple end-to-end approach, comparing various spatiotemporal self-attention layouts, focusing on causal modelling of physical simulations over time.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a simple, interpretable pure transformer model (PSViT) for end-to-end autoregressive video prediction in pixel-space, which extends the time horizon for physically accurate predictions by up to 50% compared to existing latent-space approaches.
papers.conclusion: The presented simple, interpretable pure transformer for end-to-end autoregressive video prediction extends the horizon for physically accurate predictions while maintaining competitive performance on standard video quality metrics, highlighting the benefits of a straightforward end-to-end approach.
papers.key_findings:
The PSViT model achieves increased temporal accuracy in predicting PDE-driven video sequences compared to existing approaches, as measured by an object tracking metric.
The model maintains competitive performance on standard video quality metrics (SSIM, PSNR).
Interpretability experiments identify network regions that encode information useful for estimating PDE simulation parameters via probing.
The learned encoding of underlying physics generalizes to the estimation of out-of-distribution simulation parameters.
The model's performance is evaluated on several physics simulation datasets and common video prediction benchmarks.
papers.limitation:
For three of the simulation datasets increasing PSViT model size has minimal impact on performance over time.
For stochastic video-generation results on BAIR, the approach falls short compared to latent space models.
Object shapes, although positioned accurately, can distort over time, particularly when rotation is involved.
By performing end-to-end training, the model doesn't benefit from the large-scale pretrained image encoders/decoders often employed by latent space models.
future_direction: Developing more sophisticated metrics for evaluating physical accuracy, moving beyond current object-based pixel distance methods.
Training larger models on higher-resolution datasets featuring increased visual fidelity and physical complexity.
papers.abstract: Inspired by the performance and scalability of autoregressive large language models (LLMs), transformer-based models have seen recent success in the visual domain. This study investigates a transformer adaptation for video prediction with a simple end-to-end approach, comparing various spatiotemporal self-attention layouts. Focusing on causal modeling of physical simulations over time; a common shortcoming of existing video-generative approaches, we attempt to isolate spatiotemporal reasoning via physical object tracking metrics and unsupervised training on physical simulation datasets. We introduce a simple yet effective pure transformer model for autoregressive video prediction, utilizing continuous pixel-space representations for video prediction. Without the need for complex training strategies or latent feature-learning components, our approach significantly extends the time horizon for physically accurate predictions by up to 50% when compared with existing latent-space approaches, while maintaining comparable performance on common video quality metrics. In addition, we conduct interpretability experiments to identify network regions that encode information useful to perform accurate estimations of PDE simulation parameters via probing models, and find that this generalizes to the estimation of out-of-distribution simulation parameters. This work serves as a platform for further attention-based spatiotemporal modeling of videos via a simple, parameter efficient, and interpretable approach.

papers.title: Unboxing the Black Box: Mechanistic Interpretability for Algorithmic Understanding of Neural Networks
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a unified taxonomy of mechanistic interpretability approaches, situates MI within the broader XAI landscape, and surveys key techniques and literature in the field.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that mechanistic interpretability holds significant potential to support a more scientific understanding of machine learning systems and invites new researchers into the field.
papers.key_findings:
The field of mechanistic interpretability has grown rapidly since 2020.
MI faces challenges such as superposition, spurious correlations, scalability, and evaluation problems.
MI offers opportunities for debugging, data privacy, robustness, control, human-in-the-loop, and trustworthiness.
future_direction: The need for standardized evaluation techniques.
Scaling up MI techniques to larger models.
Applying MI in real-world domains like finance and medicine.
papers.abstract: The black box nature of deep neural networks poses a significant challenge for the deployment of transparent and trustworthy artificial intelligence (AI) systems. With the growing presence of AI in society, it becomes increasingly important to develop methods that can explain and interpret the decisions made by these systems. To address this, mechanistic interpretability (MI) emerged as a promising and distinctive research program within the broader field of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). MI is the process of studying the inner computations of neural networks and translating them into human-understandable algorithms. It encompasses reverse engineering techniques aimed at uncovering the computational algorithms implemented by neural networks. In this article, we propose a unified taxonomy of MI approaches and provide a detailed analysis of key techniques, illustrated with concrete examples and pseudo-code. We contextualize MI within the broader interpretability landscape, comparing its goals, methods, and insights to other strands of XAI. Additionally, we trace the development of MI as a research area, highlighting its conceptual roots and the accelerating pace of recent work. We argue that MI holds significant potential to support a more scientific understanding of machine learning systems -- treating models not only as tools for solving tasks, but also as systems to be studied and understood. We hope to invite new researchers into the field of mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: On interpretability and proper latent decomposition of autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we theoretically interpret the transformations of an autoencoder and generalize proper orthogonal decomposition to the autoencoder latent space for turbulent flows?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a theoretical interpretation of autoencoders using Riemannian geometry and proposes proper latent decomposition (PLD), which generalizes proper orthogonal decomposition to the curved latent space of autoencoders for turbulent flows.
papers.conclusion: The paper sets up a theoretical framework to interpret autoencoders and to decompose turbulent flows with PLD, with future work focused on computational implementation and assessment.
papers.key_findings:
The latent space of an autoencoder is a curved manifold with curvilinear coordinates.
The metric tensor of the latent space can be derived from the decoder, providing a mathematical description of the manifold.
Proper latent decomposition (PLD) generalizes proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) to the curved latent space, finding dominant directions.
The mean and covariance on the latent space can be defined using Riemannian geometry, specifically the Fréchet mean and logarithmic map.
PLD enables the creation of reduced-order models of turbulent flows on the learned latent manifold.
future_direction: Translating the theoretical framework into a computational framework.
Assessment of the physical insight gained from the proper latent modes.
Accuracy of the reduced-order models from PLD.
papers.abstract: The dynamics of a turbulent flow tend to occupy only a portion of the phase space at a statistically stationary regime. From a dynamical systems point of view, this portion is the attractor. The knowledge of the turbulent attractor is useful for two purposes, at least: (i) We can gain physical insight into turbulence (what is the shape and geometry of the attractor?), and (ii) it provides the minimal number of degrees of freedom to accurately describe the turbulent dynamics. Autoencoders enable the computation of an optimal latent space, which is a low-order representation of the dynamics. If properly trained and correctly designed, autoencoders can learn an approximation of the turbulent attractor, as shown by Doan, Racca and Magri (2022). In this paper, we theoretically interpret the transformations of an autoencoder. First, we remark that the latent space is a curved manifold with curvilinear coordinates, which can be analyzed with simple tools from Riemann geometry. Second, we characterize the geometrical properties of the latent space. We mathematically derive the metric tensor, which provides a mathematical description of the manifold. Third, we propose a method -- proper latent decomposition (PLD) -- that generalizes proper orthogonal decomposition of turbulent flows on the autoencoder latent space. This decomposition finds the dominant directions in the curved latent space. This theoretical work opens up computational opportunities for interpreting autoencoders and creating reduced-order models of turbulent flows.

papers.title: PAHQ: Accelerating Automated Circuit Discovery through Mixed-Precision Inference Optimization
papers.research_question: How can automated circuit discovery be accelerated while maintaining faithfulness, addressing its computational inefficiency and high memory requirements?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PAHQ, a training-free mixed-precision quantization method that accelerates automated circuit discovery by maintaining high precision for critical attention heads and reducing precision elsewhere, achieving significant speedup and memory reduction with minimal faithfulness loss.
papers.conclusion: PAHQ provides an efficient acceleration approach for mechanistic interpretability research without sacrificing analytical quality, making circuit discovery more computationally feasible.
papers.key_findings:
PAHQ-accelerated ACDC reduces runtime by up to 80% and memory consumption by up to 30% compared to unaccelerated ACDC while maintaining faithfulness.
PAHQ outperforms RTN quantization and Edge Attribution Patching (EAP) in terms of AUC-ROC on circuit discovery tasks like IOI, Docstring, and Greater Than.
The method is training-free and readily integrates with existing edge-based circuit discovery techniques by modifying the attention computation mechanism.
PAHQ's selective precision allocation and three-stream parallel scheduler effectively mask data transfer latency, enabling near-optimal throughput.
The method scales effectively to larger transformer models (GPT-2-medium, large, XL) while maintaining competitive performance.
papers.limitation:
PAHQ is designed for algorithms that evaluate edges sequentially (like ACDC) and may not be as effective for methods that evaluate multiple edges simultaneously (like EAP).
PAHQ makes circuit discovery more feasible for moderately larger models but does not solve the scalability challenge for foundation models with hundreds of billions of parameters.
The method is empirically validated but lacks theoretical analysis on how high-precision signals propagate through lower-precision layers.
papers.abstract: Circuit discovery, which involves identifying sparse and task-relevant subnetworks in pre-trained language models, is a cornerstone of mechanistic interpretability. Automated Circuit Discovery (ACDC) has emerged as a pivotal methodology in circuit discovery, but its application to large language models is severely limited by computational inefficiency and prohibitively high memory requirements. Although several accelerated approaches have been proposed, they primarily rely on linear approximations to ACDC, which significantly compromises analytical faithfulness. Our proposed method for accelerating automated circuit discovery, Per Attention Head Quantization (PAHQ), takes a fundamentally different approach by optimizing the efficiency of each individual patching operation. PAHQ leverages a fundamental alignment between activation patching and mixed-precision quantization (MPQ): interpretability analysis through patching essentially performs targeted ablation studies. Therefore, we can maintain high precision exclusively for investigated components while safely reducing precision elsewhere in the network. PAHQ-accelerated ACDC reduces runtime by up to 80\% and memory consumption by up to 30\% compared to unaccelerated ACDC while maintaining faithfulness. Importantly, our method readily integrates with existing edge-based circuit discovery techniques by modifying the attention computation mechanism. This training-free approach provides a practical and novel pathway for accelerating mechanistic interpretability methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/626619403/PAHQ.

papers.title: Using Causal Analysis for Conceptual Deep Learning Explanation
papers.research_question: How to provide clinically relevant explanations for deep learning models in healthcare by associating hidden units with concepts and using causal analysis to ensure influence.
papers.core_contribution: A framework for explaining black-box models using clinically relevant concepts and causal mediation analysis to ensure concepts causally influence the model's decisions.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework provides global explanations for black-box models in terms of clinically relevant concepts that are causally influencing the model's decisions.
papers.key_findings:
Concept classifiers using sparse logistic regression achieve high recall, indicating effective association of hidden units with concepts.
Hidden units act as visual concept detectors, localizing radiographic features without explicit concept supervision during training.
Causal mediation analysis via counterfactual interventions ranks concepts based on indirect effect, with top-ranked concepts being clinically consistent.
The indirect effect is highest in middle layers (dense-block 3), showing their role in mediating decisions.
A decision tree surrogate function provides interpretable global explanations using the top-ranked concepts.
future_direction: Extend concept definition to include a broader set of clinical metrics.

papers.title: Rethinking the Role of Scale for In-Context Learning: An Interpretability-based Case Study at 66 Billion Scale
papers.research_question: Are all LLM components really needed to perform in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: Only a core nucleus of attention heads and feed forward networks (FFNs) in a large language model (OPT-66B) are important for in-context learning across a wide variety of tasks, and these important heads overlap with task-agnostic induction heads.
papers.conclusion: Large language models may be undertrained for in-context learning, and the findings motivate investigating pre-training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
~70% of attention heads and ~20% of FFNs can be removed with minimal decline in in-context learning task performance.
Important attention heads are primarily clustered in the intermediate layers of the model.
There is substantial overlap in the set of attention heads (un)important for in-context learning across tasks and number of in-context examples (shots).
A small set of attention heads in OPT-66B score highly on primitive induction operations (prefix matching and copying).
These induction heads overlap with task-specific important heads, indicating they are capable of more sophisticated in-context learning behaviors.
papers.limitation:
No causal link is claimed between induction heads and sophisticated in-context learning capabilities; deeper investigation is needed.
The study uses only up to 5 in-context examples and random selection of examples.
All downstream tasks are monolingual.
future_direction: Increase the number and strength of induction heads via auxiliary pre-training objectives for primitives like prefix matching and copying.
Investigate and improve (pre-)training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
Replicate the study with instruction-tuned model variants (e.g., OPT-IML).
papers.abstract: Hritik Bansal, Karthik Gopalakrishnan, Saket Dingliwal, Sravan Bodapati, Katrin Kirchhoff, Dan Roth. Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2023.

papers.title: Interpretable Neural System Dynamics: Combining Deep Learning with System Dynamics Modeling to Support Critical Applications
papers.research_question: How can an interpretable neural system dynamics framework ensure transparency and accountability while maintaining the predictive power of deep learning, and how can methods from concept-based interpretability, causal learning, and mechanistic interpretability be integrated to achieve this?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an Interpretable Neural System Dynamics pipeline that integrates concept-based interpretability, causal machine learning, and mechanistic interpretability to combine deep learning's scalability with system dynamics' interpretability and causal reliability.
papers.conclusion: The research aims to bridge the gap between theoretical explainable AI and real-world applications, providing a framework for interpretable, trustworthy AI in critical domains like transportation.
future_direction: State-of-the-art analysis of interpretability methods
Design and implementation of the INSD pipeline
Validation on real-world AutoMoTIF application
papers.abstract: The objective of this proposal is to bridge the gap between Deep Learning (DL) and System Dynamics (SD) by developing an interpretable neural system dynamics framework. While DL excels at learning complex models and making accurate predictions, it lacks interpretability and causal reliability. Traditional SD approaches, on the other hand, provide transparency and causal insights but are limited in scalability and require extensive domain knowledge. To overcome these limitations, this project introduces a Neural System Dynamics pipeline, integrating Concept-Based Interpretability, Mechanistic Interpretability, and Causal Machine Learning. This framework combines the predictive power of DL with the interpretability of traditional SD models, resulting in both causal reliability and scalability. The efficacy of the proposed pipeline will be validated through real-world applications of the EU-funded AutoMoTIF project, which is focused on autonomous multimodal transportation systems. The long-term goal is to collect actionable insights that support the integration of explainability and safety in autonomous systems.

papers.title: LLaVA Steering: Visual Instruction Tuning with 500x Fewer Parameters through Modality Linear Representation-Steering
papers.research_question: How can the number of trainable parameters for visual instruction tuning in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) be significantly reduced by addressing the intrinsic imbalance between text and visual modalities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Modality Linear Representation-Steering (MoReS), a method that rebalances text and visual modalities in MLLMs by steering visual representations through linear transformations, achieving comparable performance to LoRA with 500x fewer trainable parameters.
papers.conclusion: MoReS provides an efficient and effective approach for visual instruction tuning in MLLMs by addressing modality imbalance, significantly reducing parameter count while maintaining performance, and offering a pathway for more accessible and customizable multimodal model development.
papers.key_findings:
MoReS requires 287 to 1,150 times fewer trainable parameters than LoRA while maintaining competitive performance on multiple visual benchmarks.
MoReS effectively rebalances the attention distribution between visual and textual representations, mitigating the intrinsic modality imbalance in MLLMs.
The method reduces hallucination in MLLMs, as shown by improved performance on POPE and HallucinationBench.
MoReS preserves the LLM's pre-trained world knowledge and performs well on text-only tasks, demonstrating its generalizability.
A dynamic steering ratio mechanism allows MoReS to adapt to tasks of varying complexity, with optimal ratios differing per dataset.
papers.abstract: Jinhe Bi, Yujun Wang, Haokun Chen, Xun Xiao, Artur Hecker, Volker Tresp, Yunpu Ma. Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: Investigation of Internal Functioning of the Radial-Basis-Function Neural Network River Flow Forecasting Models
papers.research_question: Can hydrological knowledge be extracted from Radial Basis Function Neural Networks (RBFNNs) by interpreting their internal functioning, specifically by examining the responses of hidden layer neurons to understand how they represent flow components in river flow forecasting?
papers.core_contribution: The hidden neurons in an RBFNN for river flow forecasting are not arbitrary but represent specific flow components (baseflow, interflow, surface runoff), demonstrating that hydrological knowledge can be extracted from the model's internal functioning.
papers.conclusion: The RBFNN can be used as an effective flow forecasting tool, and its hidden neurons activate in a way that corresponds to hydrological flow components, suggesting that the network's internal functioning is interpretable and can extract meaningful hydrological knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
The RBFNN is an effective tool for daily flow forecasting.
The activation of hidden nodes is not arbitrary; each node dominates in one of the flow domains (low, medium, high) and represents flow components resembling baseflow, interflow, and surface runoff.
The proportional contribution from each hidden neuron varies over time, reflecting dominance in specific flow ranges.
The RBFNN parameters (centers, spreads, weights) function to decompose the flow hydrograph into meaningful components.
The method provides insight into the internal functioning of RBFNNs, showing they can mimic local models corresponding to hydrological processes.
papers.limitation: The study uses a limited number of catchments, so the findings may not generalize to all catchments.
future_direction: Apply the methodology to a large number of catchments with different characteristics.
Investigate the sensitivity of the number of RBFs and network structure to represent physical processes.
papers.abstract: This paper deals with the challenging problem of hydrological interpretation of the internal functioning of artificial neural networks (ANNs) by extracting knowledge from their solutions. The neural network used in this study is based on the structure of the radial-basis-function neural network (RBFNN), which is considered as an alternative to the multilayer perceptron for solving complex modeling problems. This network consists of input, hidden, and output layers. The network is trained using the daily data of two catchments having different characteristics and from two different regions in the world. The present day and antecedent observed discharges are used as inputs to the network to forecast the flow one day ahead. A range of quantitative and qualitative techniques are used for hydrological interpretation of the internal functioning by examining the responses of the hidden layer nodes. The results of the study show that a single hidden layered RBFNN is an effective tool to forecast the daily flows and that the activation of the hidden layer nodes are far from arbitrary, but appear to represent flow components of the predicted hydrograph. The results of the study confirm that the three nodes in the hidden layer of this model effectively divide the input data space in such a way that the contribution from each node dominates in one of the flow domains—low, medium, or high—and form, in a crude manner, the base flow, interflow and surface runoff components of the hydrograph.

papers.title: BlackboxNLP-2025 MIB Shared Task: Improving Circuit Faithfulness via Better Edge Selection
papers.research_question: How to improve circuit faithfulness via better edge selection in circuit discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes bootstrapping, positive-negative ratio (PNR), and integer linear programming (ILP) for edge selection in circuit discovery, improving faithfulness over prior methods.
papers.conclusion: Principled edge selection improves faithfulness and enables more robust circuit discovery, despite computational limitations.
papers.key_findings:
Bootstrapping identifies edges with consistent attribution scores, filtering out unstable ones.
Positive-negative ratio (PNR) selection balances positive and negative edges, improving circuit faithfulness.
Integer linear programming (ILP) provides globally optimal edge selection compared to greedy algorithms.
Combinations of these methods outperform baseline approaches across multiple models and tasks on MIB metrics.
papers.limitation:
ILP optimization scales poorly with edge count, limiting applicability to larger models.
Optimal ratio of positive edges varies by models and tasks, requiring task-specific tuning.
Gap between state-of-the-art attribution methods and 'ground truth' edge importance scores limits faithfulness gains from ILP.
papers.abstract: One of the main challenges in mechanistic interpretability is circuit discovery, determining which parts of a model perform a given task. We build on the Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark (MIB) and propose three key improvements to circuit discovery. First, we use bootstrapping to identify edges with consistent attribution scores. Second, we introduce a simple ratio-based selection strategy to prioritize strong positive-scoring edges, balancing performance and faithfulness. Third, we replace the standard greedy selection with an integer linear programming formulation. Our methods yield more faithful circuits and outperform prior approaches across multiple MIB tasks and models. Our code is available at: https://github.com/technion-cs-nlp/MIB-Shared-Task.

papers.title: Expressive architectures enhance interpretability of dynamics-based neural population models
papers.research_question: Does NODE-based sequential autoencoders more accurately and parsimoniously recover latent dynamical systems from simulated neural activity compared to RNN-based models?
papers.core_contribution: NODE-based sequential autoencoders can recover accurate and parsimonious latent dynamics from simulated neural activity, outperforming RNN-based models in interpretability.
papers.conclusion: NODE-based architectures are superior for interpretable neural population modeling due to their ability to learn accurate dynamics in low-dimensional latent spaces.
papers.key_findings:
NODE-based SAEs achieve similar reconstruction performance with fewer latent dimensions than GRU-based SAEs.
NODE-based SAEs have higher state R^2, indicating better recovery of true latent dynamics without superfluous features.
NODE-based SAEs more effectively recover fixed point properties and eigenvalues of the dynamical systems.
Ablation experiments show that skip connections and MLP capacity in NODEs are key to their superior performance.
RNN-based models struggle to recover accurate dynamics even when they have high reconstruction performance.
papers.limitation:
Global dynamics may be underdetermined from limited sampled trajectories, affecting fixed point recovery.
Models with best reconstruction performance may not concisely capture true dynamics, especially in chaotic systems.
Applicability to real neural data with time-varying dynamics and external inputs is uncertain.
future_direction: Extending the approach to real neural data with inputs and time-varying dynamics.
Testing recovery on partially observed and interacting dynamical systems.
Incorporating techniques from models like LFADS while preserving interpretability.
papers.abstract: Artificial neural networks that can recover latent dynamics from recorded neural activity may provide a powerful avenue for identifying and interpreting the dynamical motifs underlying biological computation. Given that neural variance alone does not uniquely determine a latent dynamical system, interpretable architectures should prioritize accurate and low-dimensional latent dynamics. In this work, we evaluated the performance of sequential autoencoders (SAEs) in recovering latent chaotic attractors from simulated neural datasets. We found that SAEs with widely-used recurrent neural network (RNN)-based dynamics were unable to infer accurate firing rates at the true latent state dimensionality, and that larger RNNs relied upon dynamical features not present in the data. On the other hand, SAEs with neural ordinary differential equation (NODE)-based dynamics inferred accurate rates at the true latent state dimensionality, while also recovering latent trajectories and fixed point structure. Ablations reveal that this is mainly because NODEs (1) allow use of higher-capacity multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) to model the vector field and (2) predict the derivative rather than the next state. Decoupling the capacity of the dynamics model from its latent dimensionality enables NODEs to learn the requisite low-D dynamics where RNN cells fail. Additionally, the fact that the NODE predicts derivatives imposes a useful autoregressive prior on the latent states. The suboptimal interpretability of widely-used RNN-based dynamics may motivate substitution for alternative architectures, such as NODE, that enable learning of accurate dynamics in low-dimensional latent spaces.

papers.title: Text-Trained LLMs Can Zero-Shot Extrapolate PDE Dynamics, Revealing a Three-Stage In-Context Learning Mechanism
papers.research_question: Can text-trained LLMs zero-shot extrapolate PDE dynamics, and what is the in-context learning mechanism behind this capability?
papers.core_contribution: Text-trained LLMs can zero-shot extrapolate PDE dynamics, and the in-context learning process follows a three-stage progression from syntax imitation to exploratory high-entropy phase to confident prediction.
papers.conclusion: Text-trained LLMs exhibit emergent zero-shot capability to extrapolate PDE dynamics, and the in-context learning process follows a consistent three-stage progression, revealing inductive biases analogous to numerical methods.
papers.key_findings:
One-step prediction accuracy improves with longer temporal context but degrades with finer spatial discretization.
Multi-step rollouts show algebraic error growth with time horizon, similar to classical numerical solvers.
Token-level entropy analysis reveals a three-stage ICL progression: syntax imitation, exploratory high-entropy phase, and confident prediction.
LLMs can sustain coherent multi-step rollouts for nonlinear PDEs like Allen-Cahn and wave equations.
The three-stage progression is consistent across model sizes and PDE types.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated emergent in-context learning (ICL) capabilities across a range of tasks, including zero-shot time-series forecasting. We show that text-trained foundation models can accurately extrapolate spatiotemporal dynamics from discretized partial differential equation (PDE) solutions without fine-tuning or natural language prompting. Predictive accuracy improves with longer temporal contexts but degrades at finer spatial discretizations. In multi-step rollouts, where the model recursively predicts future spatial states over multiple time steps, errors grow algebraically with the time horizon, reminiscent of global error accumulation in classical finite-difference solvers. We interpret these trends as in-context neural scaling laws, where prediction quality varies predictably with both context length and output length. To better understand how LLMs are able to internally process PDE solutions so as to accurately roll them out, we analyze token-level output distributions and uncover a consistent three-stage ICL progression: beginning with syntactic pattern imitation, transitioning through an exploratory high-entropy phase, and culminating in confident, numerically grounded predictions.

papers.title: Circuit Fingerprints: How Answer Tokens Encode Their Geometrical Path
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether circuit discovery and activation steering are two views of the same underlying geometric structure, and whether answer tokens encode the directions that would produce them.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Circuit Fingerprint hypothesis, showing that answer tokens encode the geometric directions of their generating circuits, enabling gradient-free circuit discovery and activation steering as dual operations on the same geometric structure.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that circuit discovery and activation steering are dual operations on the same geometric structure encoded in activation space, enabling gradient-free circuit discovery and effective steering, and revealing transformer circuits as geometric objects.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit membership can be determined from geometric alignment with answer token directions, recovering circuit structure comparable to gradient-based methods without backpropagation.
The same directions enable controlled steering, validating that they manipulate genuine computational pathways.
Feature circuits can be discovered by extracting directions from instruction-modified prompts, without task-specific datasets.
The method achieves comparable circuit discovery performance to gradient-based methods (EAP, EAP-IG) on IOI, SVA, and MCQA tasks across four model families.
Steering using these directions achieves 69.8% emotion classification accuracy versus 53.1% for instruction prompting while preserving factual accuracy (89.6%).
papers.limitation:
Zero-shot steering remains fragile; even grammatically correct outputs can exhibit semantic degradation.
Steering can disrupt factual recall, particularly for negative-valence emotions and distant language pairs, suggesting some features remain entangled with semantic content.
future_direction: Address position-level effects beyond the final token.
Address LayerNorm nonlinearities in edge attribution.
Develop methods to preserve factual grounding during steering.
Develop more robust persona-based circuit discovery.
papers.abstract: Circuit discovery and activation steering in transformers have developed as separate research threads, yet both operate on the same representational space. Are they two views of the same underlying structure? We show they follow a single geometric principle: answer tokens, processed in isolation, encode the directions that would produce them. This Circuit Fingerprint hypothesis enables circuit discovery without gradients or causal intervention -- recovering comparable structure to gradient-based methods through geometric alignment alone. We validate this on standard benchmarks (IOI, SVA, MCQA) across four model families, achieving circuit discovery performance comparable to gradient-based methods. The same directions that identify circuit components also enable controlled steering -- achieving 69.8\% emotion classification accuracy versus 53.1\% for instruction prompting while preserving factual accuracy. Beyond method development, this read-write duality reveals that transformer circuits are fundamentally geometric structures: interpretability and controllability are two facets of the same object.

papers.title: Circuits, Features, and Heuristics in Molecular Transformers
papers.research_question: How do autoregressive transformers trained on drug-like molecules capture the rules of molecular representation and maintain syntactic and chemical validity during generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a mechanistic analysis of an autoregressive transformer trained on drug-like molecules, identifying specialized circuits for syntactic and chemical validity and using sparse autoencoders to extract chemically meaningful features that enhance downstream predictive performance.
papers.conclusion: Molecular transformers develop specialized mechanisms for maintaining syntactic and chemical validity, and sparse autoencoders can disentangle these representations into interpretable features that are useful for downstream tasks and controllable generation.
papers.key_findings:
Identification of attention heads that implement ring and branch syntax circuits, with a division of labor between pointer and writer heads for ring closure.
Discovery of a linearly decodable valence capacity representation in the residual stream that can be steered to modulate bond predictions.
Extraction of sparse feature dictionaries via SAEs that align with chemically meaningful substructures, enabled by an automated fragment-screening pipeline.
Demonstration that SAE-derived features improve transformer embeddings on property prediction tasks, competitive with traditional fingerprints.
SAE features can be used for steering generation towards desired chemical structures.
papers.limitation: Steering with SAE features can degrade validity for complex targets and the effects are not uniform, indicating that SAE latents are preliminary control knobs rather than fully-fledged conditional generators.
papers.abstract: Transformers generate valid and diverse chemical structures, but little is known about the mechanisms that enable these models to capture the rules of molecular representation. We present a mechanistic analysis of autoregressive transformers trained on drug-like small molecules to reveal the computational structure underlying their capabilities across multiple levels of abstraction. We identify computational patterns consistent with low-level syntactic parsing and more abstract chemical validity constraints. Using sparse autoencoders (SAEs), we extract feature dictionaries associated with chemically relevant activation patterns. We validate our findings on downstream tasks and find that mechanistic insights can translate to predictive performance in various practical settings.

papers.title: Operationally meaningful representations of physical systems in neural networks
papers.research_question: How can we design neural networks to learn operationally meaningful representations of physical systems that separate parameters relevant for different experimental settings?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neural network architecture that learns operationally meaningful representations of physical systems by imposing a communication efficiency criterion between agents, leading to disentangled parameters that correspond to physically relevant quantities.
papers.conclusion: The proposed architecture can learn operationally meaningful representations that separate physically relevant parameters, and it can be combined with reinforcement learning for interactive settings.
papers.key_findings:
The architecture can separate local parameters from interaction parameters in classical charged particle systems.
It can separate local qubit parameters from quantum correlation parameters in two-qubit systems.
The method can be combined with reinforcement learning to learn representations in interactive scenarios.
future_direction: Combining the method with reinforcement learning for more complex environments.
Exploring other operational criteria for representation learning.
papers.abstract: Abstract To make progress in science, we often build abstract representations of physical systems that meaningfully encode information about the systems.
