Such representations ignore redundant features and treat parameters such as velocity and position separately because they can be useful for making statements about different experimental settings. Here, we capture this notion by formally defining the concept of operationally meaningful representations. We present an autoencoder architecture with attention mechanism that can generate such representations and demonstrate it on examples involving both classical and quantum physics. For instance, our architecture finds a compact representation of an arbitrary two-qubit system that separates local parameters from parameters describing quantum correlations.

papers.title: Additive-feature-attribution methods: a review on explainable artificial intelligence for fluid dynamics and heat transfer
papers.core_contribution: This review paper summarizes the application of additive-feature-attribution methods (SHAP) in fluid dynamics and heat transfer, highlighting their importance for interpretable and physics-compliant deep-learning models.
papers.conclusion: This review shows that explainability techniques, and in particular additive-feature-attribution methods, are crucial for implementing interpretable and physics-compliant deep-learning models in the fluid-mechanics field.
papers.key_findings:
Additive-feature-attribution methods are crucial for implementing interpretable and physics-compliant deep-learning models in fluid mechanics.
SHAP values provide a unique solution for understanding the model by linking input features with the model prediction.
The review categorizes applications into turbulence modeling, fluid-mechanics fundamentals, and applied problems in fluid dynamics and heat transfer.
papers.abstract: The use of data-driven methods in fluid mechanics has surged dramatically in recent years due to their capacity to adapt to the complex and multi-scale nature of turbulent flows, as well as to detect patterns in large-scale simulations or experimental tests. In order to interpret the relationships generated in the models during the training process, numerical attributions need to be assigned to the input features. One important example are the additive-feature-attribution methods. These explainability methods link the input features with the model prediction, providing an interpretation based on a linear formulation of the models. The SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP values) are formulated as the only possible interpretation that offers a unique solution for understanding the model. In this manuscript, the additive-feature-attribution methods are presented, showing four common implementations in the literature: kernel SHAP, tree SHAP, gradient SHAP, and deep SHAP. Then, the main applications of the additive-feature-attribution methods are introduced, dividing them into three main groups: turbulence modeling, fluid-mechanics fundamentals, and applied problems in fluid dynamics and heat transfer. This review shows thatexplainability techniques, and in particular additive-feature-attribution methods, are crucial for implementing interpretable and physics-compliant deep-learning models in the fluid-mechanics field.

papers.title: Generalizing biological surround suppression based on center surround similarity via deep neural network models
papers.research_question: How do feedforward deep convolutional neural networks exhibit and generalize surround suppression effects based on center-surround similarity, and how do they compare to biological neurons?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that feedforward convolutional neural networks exhibit surround suppression based on center-surround similarity, similar to biological V1 neurons, and introduces a gradient-based visualization method to generalize these effects to complex stimuli.
papers.conclusion: The findings generalize surround suppression to complex stimuli, providing testable hypotheses for higher visual cortices, and the visualization approach offers a new paradigm for biological experiments.
papers.key_findings:
CNNs show that the most suppressive surround orientation matches the center orientation, akin to V1 neurons.
Visualization reveals that for complex stimuli, the most suppressive surround is visually similar to the center.
In late layers, the most suppressive surround can follow changes in the center stimulus.
These effects are not present in untrained networks, indicating the role of learning.
Mismatches with biology include lack of geometric dependency in surround suppression and differences in contrast effects.
papers.limitation:
Feedforward CNNs lack clear center-surround separation and do not capture all biological surround effects, such as geometric dependencies.
CNNs show mismatches in contrast-dependent effects compared to cortical neurons.
future_direction: Elucidating the abstract mathematical form of surround effects in CNNs.
Incorporating scene statistics and divisive normalization into deep neural networks.
Testing hypotheses about efficient coding and high-order spatial dependencies.
papers.abstract: Sensory perception is dramatically influenced by the context. Models of contextual neural surround effects in vision have mostly accounted for Primary Visual Cortex (V1) data, via nonlinear computations such as divisive normalization. However, surround effects are not well understood within a hierarchy, for neurons with more complex stimulus selectivity beyond V1. We utilized feedforward deep convolutional neural networks and developed a gradient-based technique to visualize the most suppressive and excitatory surround. We found that deep neural networks exhibited a key signature of surround effects in V1, highlighting center stimuli that visually stand out from the surround and suppressing responses when the surround stimulus is similar to the center. We found that in some neurons, especially in late layers, when the center stimulus was altered, the most suppressive surround surprisingly can follow the change. Through the visualization approach, we generalized previous understanding of surround effects to more complex stimuli, in ways that have not been revealed in visual cortices. In contrast, the suppression based on center surround similarity was not observed in an untrained network. We identified further successes and mismatches of the feedforward CNNs to the biology. Our results provide a testable hypothesis of surround effects in higher visual cortices, and the visualization approach could be adopted in future biological experimental designs.

papers.title: LLMs learn governing principles of dynamical systems, revealing an in-context neural scaling law
papers.research_question: Can LLMs learn the governing principles of dynamical systems from in-context data, and does the accuracy of learned rules scale with context length?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs can learn the probabilistic transition rules of various dynamical systems from in-context data without fine-tuning, and the accuracy of the learned rules follows a power-law scaling with context length, revealing an in-context neural scaling law.
papers.conclusion: Pretrained LLMs can accurately recover the probabilistic transition rules underlying deterministic, chaotic, and stochastic time series when provided with sufficient context, and this learning follows an in-context scaling law.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs (LLaMA-13b, LLaMA-70b) can accurately predict the next state in time series from stochastic, chaotic, continuous, and discrete dynamical systems without any fine-tuning or prompt engineering.
The discrepancy between the learned transition rules and ground truth decreases as a power law with the length of the observed time series, indicating an in-context neural scaling law.
The introduced Hierarchy-PDF algorithm efficiently extracts probability density functions for multi-digit numbers from LLM predictions.
For deterministic systems, the squared deviations from the mean (SDM) loss is more stable than the Bhattacharyya distance for capturing learning dynamics.
LLMs can learn both the mean and variance of next-state distributions for stochastic systems, as demonstrated on the noisy logistic map and geometric Brownian motion.
papers.limitation:
Although unlikely, the possibility of data leakage (memorization) cannot be completely ruled out and requires rigorous testing in future work.
The study does not evaluate newer models like LLaMA-3 due to time and computational constraints, limiting the comprehensiveness of the findings.
future_direction: Investigating how LLMs encode spatio-temporal features in stochastic dynamical time series and how they represent the learned transition rules.
Examining how LLMs perform subtasks necessary for learning stochastic dynamical systems, such as collecting Markovian transition statistics from discrete data and performing density estimation.
Assessing to what extent training on natural language enhances a transformer's mathematical ability to in-context learn dynamical systems, and vice-versa.
papers.abstract: Pretrained large language models (LLMs) are surprisingly effective at performing zero-shot tasks, including time-series forecasting. However, understanding the mechanisms behind such capabilities remains highly challenging due to the complexity of the models. We study LLMs' ability to extrapolate the behavior of dynamical systems whose evolution is governed by principles of physical interest. Our results show that LLaMA 2, a language model trained primarily on texts, achieves accurate predictions of dynamical system time series without fine-tuning or prompt engineering. Moreover, the accuracy of the learned physical rules increases with the length of the input context window, revealing an in-context version of neural scaling law. Along the way, we present a flexible and efficient algorithm for extracting probability density functions of multi-digit numbers directly from LLMs.

papers.title: Challenges in Mechanistically Interpreting Model Representations
papers.research_question: What are the challenges in mechanistically interpreting model representations, and how do current mechanistic interpretability tools fall short in understanding complex behaviors like dishonesty?
papers.core_contribution: The paper formalizes the importance of studying feature and behavior representations in models, performs an exploratory study of dishonesty representations in Mistral-7B, and shows that current mechanistic interpretability tools are insufficient for understanding such representations, advocating for new frameworks.
papers.conclusion: Studying representations for features and behaviors is crucial for understanding models, but current mechanistic interpretability tooling is inadequate for answering key questions about representations, necessitating new frameworks.
papers.key_findings:
Linear representations for dishonesty can be found and used to steer model behavior, but they are not simply boosting generically dishonest tokens.
Continual injections of the dishonesty direction are required for open-ended dishonest generation, not just at the first token.
Direct logit attribution shows that directional injections affect many components, with MLPs having a more direct effect than attention heads.
Activation patching reveals that many components are involved in the dishonesty behavior, making sparse circuit analysis difficult and less helpful.
Current mechanistic interpretability tooling (e.g., patching) is insufficient for understanding how representations are formed and how they affect long-term generation.
papers.limitation: Patching methods (activation and path patching) do not rigorously prove that circuits found are indeed reserved to that task, and patching only one component at a time might not isolate components if multiple perform the same job.
future_direction: Study how different components interact with representations and alter them.
Explore the training dynamics of a model and study the emergence of representations as a model trains.
Develop new frameworks to think about and study representations.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability (MI) aims to understand AI models by reverse-engineering the exact algorithms neural networks learn. Most works in MI so far have studied behaviors and capabilities that are trivial and token-aligned. However, most capabilities important for safety and trust are not that trivial, which advocates for the study of hidden representations inside these networks as the unit of analysis. We formalize representations for features and behaviors, highlight their importance and evaluation, and perform an exploratory study of dishonesty representations in `Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.1'. We justify that studying representations is an important and under-studied field, and highlight several challenges that arise while attempting to do so through currently established methods in MI, showing their insufficiency and advocating work on new frameworks for the same.

papers.title: The dynamics of neural codes in biological and artificial neural networks
papers.research_question: How does the brain process information and encode external stimuli? This thesis investigates the dynamics of neural codes in biological and artificial neural networks, focusing on criticality, plasticity, and representational drift.
papers.core_contribution: This thesis demonstrates quasi-universal scaling properties in brain activity near criticality, links the dynamical regime of neural networks to the optimal topological properties of neural representations, and proposes a synaptic plasticity mechanism to explain representational drift in the olfactory cortex.
papers.conclusion: The thesis highlights the importance of interdisciplinary approaches combining physics, neuroscience, and machine learning to understand the dynamics of neural codes and their role in information processing.
papers.key_findings:
Brain activity across different regions exhibits scale-invariant properties and operates close to a critical point.
Biologically-inspired plasticity rules in reservoir computers shape the dynamical regime and can lead to transitions in forecasting performance.
Optimal neural representations of sensory stimuli require smooth manifolds, and these representations emerge at critical dynamics in neural networks.
Representational drift in the olfactory cortex can be explained by a synaptic plasticity mechanism that depends on the frequency of stimulus presentation.
papers.abstract: Advancing our knowledge of how the brain processes information remains a key challenge in neuroscience. This thesis combines three different approaches to the study of the dynamics of neural networks and their encoding representations: a computational approach, that builds upon basic biological features of neurons and their networks to construct effective models that can simulate their structure and dynamics; a machine-learning approach, which draws a parallel with the functional capabilities of brain networks, allowing us to infer the dynamical and encoding properties required to solve certain input-processing tasks; and a final, theoretical treatment, which will take us into the fascinating hypothesis of the "critical" brain as the mathematical foundation that can explain the emergent collective properties arising from the interactions of millions of neurons. Hand in hand with physics, we venture into the realm of neuroscience to explain the existence of quasi-universal scaling properties across brain regions, setting out to quantify the distance of their dynamics from a critical point. Next, we move into the grounds of artificial intelligence, where the very same theory of critical phenomena will prove very useful for explaining the effects of biologically-inspired plasticity rules in the forecasting ability of Reservoir Computers. Halfway into our journey, we explore the concept of neural representations of external stimuli, unveiling a surprising link between the dynamical regime of neural networks and the optimal topological properties of such representation manifolds. The thesis ends with the singular problem of representational drift in the process of odor encoding carried out by the olfactory cortex, uncovering the potential synaptic plasticity mechanisms that could explain this recently observed phenomenon.

papers.title: Open Problems in Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: What are the key open problems in mechanistic interpretability methods, applications, and socio-technical challenges that need to be addressed to achieve the field's goals?
papers.core_contribution: This review synthesizes and outlines key open problems in mechanistic interpretability, covering methods, applications, and socio-technical challenges to guide future research.
papers.conclusion: The review outlines critical open problems in mechanistic interpretability that must be addressed to achieve scientific and engineering goals, emphasizing the need for methodological improvements and socio-technical integration.
papers.key_findings:
Mechanistic interpretability methods, such as sparse dictionary learning, suffer from practical and conceptual limitations like high reconstruction errors and unclear theoretical foundations.
Applying interpretability to AI safety requires robust methods for monitoring internal states and controlling behavior, but current techniques are insufficient.
Socio-technical challenges include integrating interpretability into AI governance and addressing philosophical questions about the field's goals.
future_direction: Developing better decomposition methods like sparse dictionary learning with lower reconstruction errors.
Creating validation frameworks for interpretability hypotheses.
Applying interpretability to AI safety monitoring and control.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand the computational mechanisms underlying neural networks' capabilities in order to accomplish concrete scientific and engineering goals. Progress in this field thus promises to provide greater assurance over AI system behavior and shed light on exciting scientific questions about the nature of intelligence. Despite recent progress toward these goals, there are many open problems in the field that require solutions before many scientific and practical benefits can be realized: Our methods require both conceptual and practical improvements to reveal deeper insights; we must figure out how best to apply our methods in pursuit of specific goals; and the field must grapple with socio-technical challenges that influence and are influenced by our work. This forward-facing review discusses the current frontier of mechanistic interpretability and the open problems that the field may benefit from prioritizing.

papers.title: What can attribution methods show us about chemical language models?
papers.research_question: How can attribution methods be used to explain the predictions of a chemical language model for aqueous solubility?
papers.core_contribution: The adapted transformer-specific attribution method produces sparse attributions that reflect how the model maps molecular strings to its latent space, while SHAP provides sensible atom-level attributions but fails to explain functional groups relevant to solubility.
papers.conclusion: Attribution methods provide insight into how chemical language models represent molecules, but current techniques have limitations in explaining solubility predictions in terms of functional groups, instead revealing how the model organizes its latent space.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning the MegaMolBART encoder significantly improves aqueous solubility prediction accuracy.
The transformer-specific attribution method (using the hRi token) yields sparse attributions that are characteristic of how the model represents molecular similarity in its latent space.
SHAP provides chemically sensible attributions (e.g., highlighting electronegative atoms) but does not explain predictions at the level of functional groups.
The fine-tuned model's latent space becomes linearly separable with respect to solubility along the first principal component.
The transformer-specific attribution method cannot propagate negative gradient information, limiting its ability to attribute negative contributions to solubility.
papers.limitation:
The transformer-specific attribution method cannot propagate negative gradient information, preventing attribution of features that negatively contribute to solubility.
SHAP does not capture functional group-level explanations for solubility predictions.
ECFP-based models are less predictive and their explanations are coarse-grained.
future_direction: Using the attributions to design focused, informative chemical datasets by creating training examples that contravene the model's predictions.
papers.abstract: Language models trained on molecular string representations have shown strong performance in predictive and generative tasks. However, practical applications require not only making accurate predictions, but also explainability - the ability to explain the reasons and rationale behind the predictions. In this work, we explore explainability for a chemical language model by adapting a transformer-specific and a model-agnostic input attribution technique. We fine-tune a pretrained model to predict aqueous solubility, compare training and architecture variants, and evaluate visualizations of attributed relevance. The model-agnostic SHAP technique provides sensible attributions, highlighting the positive influence of individual electronegative atoms, but does not explain the model in terms of functional groups or explain how the model represents molecular strings internally to make predictions. In contrast, the adapted transformer-specific explainability technique produces sparse attributions, which cannot be directly attributed to functional groups relevant to solubility. Instead, the attributions are more characteristic of how the model maps molecular strings to its latent space, which seems to represent features relevant to molecular similarity rather than functional groups. These findings provide insight into the representations underpinning chemical language models, which we propose may be leveraged for the design of informative chemical spaces for training more accurate, advanced and explainable models.

papers.title: Towards Open-Ended Visual Scientific Discovery with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can enable open-ended feature discovery from foundation model representations.
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can systematically recover semantic structure from foundation model representations without concept supervision, enabling open-ended feature discovery for scientific exploration.
papers.conclusion: SAEs provide a practical method for extracting interpretable features from vision foundation models, supporting open-ended discovery in scientific domains where target concepts are not pre-specified.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs outperform k-means and PCA on concept alignment metrics like mAP, Purity@k, and Coverage@τ.
Matryoshka SAEs achieve higher class coverage than standard SAEs on ADE20K.
SAEs can recover fine-grained anatomical parts from ecological images without labels.
Larger foundation models and later transformer layers lead to better concept rediscovery despite being harder to reconstruct.
Concept prevalence affects rediscovery; more common parts are recovered more reliably.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation relies on ground-truth annotations to measure concept alignment, limiting assessment in truly unannotated domains.
Only visual examples are used to describe features; future work might use multimodal LLMs for language descriptions.
future_direction: Systematic evaluation of novel discoveries in unannotated domains.
Applying SAEs to non-vision foundation models.
papers.abstract: Scientific archives now contain hundreds of petabytes of data across genomics, ecology, climate, and molecular biology that could reveal undiscovered patterns if systematically analyzed at scale. Large-scale, weakly-supervised datasets in language and vision have driven the development of foundation models whose internal representations encode structure (patterns, co-occurrences and statistical regularities) beyond their training objectives. Most existing methods extract structure only for pre-specified targets; they excel at confirmation but do not support open-ended discovery of unknown patterns. We ask whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can enable open-ended feature discovery from foundation model representations. We evaluate this question in controlled rediscovery studies, where the learned SAE features are tested for alignment with semantic concepts on a standard segmentation benchmark and compared against strong label-free alternatives on concept-alignment metrics. Applied to ecological imagery, the same procedure surfaces fine-grained anatomical structure without access to segmentation or part labels, providing a scientific case study with ground-truth validation. While our experiments focus on vision with an ecology case study, the method is domain-agnostic and applicable to models in other sciences (e.g., proteins, genomics, weather). Our results indicate that sparse decomposition provides a practical instrument for exploring what scientific foundation models have learned, an important prerequisite for moving from confirmation to genuine discovery.

papers.title: Interpretation of Prediction Models Using the Input Gradient
papers.research_question: How can we interpret the behavior of any predictive model? The paper proposes using the partial derivatives of the model with respect to the input to determine which variables affect the prediction and how.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes using the gradient of the model with respect to input features as a general method to interpret which input variables affect the prediction and how.
papers.conclusion: The gradient vector with respect to input is a useful quantity for interpreting model behavior, providing insights into feature importance and revealing global structure such as linearity.
papers.key_findings:
The gradient norm with respect to word embeddings in a CNN model can identify the most influential words or expressions for sentiment classification.
For a Bag-of-Words neural network, the average gradient over the test set provides a global ranking of word importance, revealing words like 'excellent' and 'worst' as most influential.
The average gradient vector can approximate the prediction function with 99.6% accuracy, indicating the decision boundary is nearly linear.
The gradient-based interpretation method is general and can be applied to any predictive model, including non-differentiable cases via numerical approximation.
The method is computationally efficient as gradients can be obtained via backpropagation.
papers.abstract: State of the art machine learning algorithms are highly optimized to provide the optimal prediction possible, naturally resulting in complex models. While these models often outperform simpler more interpretable models by order of magnitudes, in terms of understanding the way the model functions, we are often facing a "black box". In this paper we suggest a simple method to interpret the behavior of any predictive model, both for regression and classification. Given a particular model, the information required to interpret it can be obtained by studying the partial derivatives of the model with respect to the input. We exemplify this insight by interpreting convolutional and multi-layer neural networks in the field of natural language processing.

papers.title: Attribution Patching Outperforms Automated Circuit Discovery
papers.research_question: Does a simple method based on attribution patching outperform existing automated circuit discovery methods in identifying circuits?
papers.core_contribution: Edge Attribution Patching (EAP) outperforms existing automated circuit discovery methods like ACDC in identifying circuits while being substantially faster, requiring only two forward passes and one backward pass.
papers.conclusion: Edge Attribution Patching (EAP) outperforms ACDC in identifying circuits and is faster, but its results can be improved by running ACDC on the pruned subgraph found by EAP.
papers.key_findings:
Edge Attribution Patching (EAP) has greater AUC for circuit recovery than ACDC on the IOI and Greater-Than tasks.
EAP is more efficient than activation patching, requiring only two forward passes and a backward pass.
The linear approximation of activation patching by attribution patching is not always accurate, especially when the task-specific metric is concave.
Running ACDC on the pruned subgraph returned by EAP can improve the identification of relevant edges.
Attribution scores for edges in the ground-truth circuit tend to be spread further from zero than edges not in the circuit.
papers.limitation:
The linear approximation used by attribution patching can be inaccurate, especially for edges from the model's embeddings, leading to overestimation of edge importance.
The metrics used for interpretability (e.g., circuit recovery against human-found circuits) do not precisely capture meaningful human understanding and are limited by the imperfections of human-found circuits.
future_direction: Future circuit discovery experiments should run EAP first and then apply ACDC on the pruned subgraph.

papers.title: Same Task, Different Circuits: Disentangling Modality-Specific Mechanisms in VLMs
papers.research_question: Why do Vision-Language models (VLMs) perform worse on visual tasks compared to analogous textual tasks?
papers.core_contribution: VLMs use largely disjoint circuits for visual and textual tasks, but the functional difference lies in data processing; patching visual token embeddings from later layers to earlier layers (back-patching) reduces the performance gap without training.
papers.conclusion: The performance gap in VLMs arises from disjoint circuits for different modalities, and back-patching provides a training-free method to reduce it by aligning visual representations earlier.
papers.key_findings:
Vision and language circuits are structurally disjoint but implement similar functionalities for query and generation.
The performance gap stems from differences in processing modality-specific data tokens.
Visual token representations become aligned with textual counterparts only in later layers.
Back-patching visual token embeddings from later to earlier layers improves visual task accuracy, closing about a third of the performance gap on average.
The intervention is effective across multiple models and tasks.
papers.limitation:
Focused on single-image question-answering tasks with single-token completions.
Current open models struggle with complex visual reasoning, limiting analysis.
Circuit analysis methods are limited to single-token completions.
Back-patching closes only 32% of the performance gap; causes for the remaining gap are unclear.
Analysis is limited to adapter-based VLMs; may not apply to other fusion approaches.
future_direction: Explore multi-image scenarios, different prompt orders, and more complex visual reasoning tasks.
Investigate varied computational resources per token, especially for visual inputs.
Extend analysis to VLMs with different fusion approaches.
papers.abstract: Vision-Language models (VLMs) show impressive abilities to answer questions on visual inputs (e.g., counting objects in an image), yet demonstrate higher accuracies when performing an analogous task on text (e.g., counting words in a text). We investigate this accuracy gap by identifying and comparing the \textit{circuits} - the task-specific computational sub-graphs - in different modalities. We show that while circuits are largely disjoint between modalities, they implement relatively similar functionalities: the differences lie primarily in processing modality-specific data positions (an image or a text sequence). Zooming in on the image data representations, we observe they become aligned with the higher-performing analogous textual representations only towards later layers, too late in processing to effectively influence subsequent positions. To overcome this, we patch the representations of visual data tokens from later layers back into earlier layers. In experiments with multiple tasks and models, this simple intervention closes a third of the performance gap between the modalities, on average. Our analysis sheds light on the multi-modal performance gap in VLMs and suggests a training-free approach for reducing it.

papers.title: Navigating the Latent Space Dynamics of Neural Models
papers.research_question: How can neural models, specifically autoencoders, be interpreted as dynamical systems, and what properties of the model and data can be revealed by the latent vector field and its attractors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that autoencoders implicitly define a latent vector field whose attractors encode model properties, enabling analysis of generalization and memorization, data-free probing of pretrained models, and out-of-distribution detection.
papers.conclusion: The latent vector field provides a novel and powerful representation for analyzing neural models, revealing internal properties and enabling applications like data-free probing and OOD detection.
papers.key_findings:
Autoencoders define a latent vector field whose attractors correspond to memorized data points or generalized representations, depending on regularization.
During training, the model transitions from memorization to generalization, which is reflected in the evolution of attractors.
Attractors computed from Gaussian noise can recover semantic information from pretrained vision foundation models without any input data.
Trajectories in the latent vector field can distinguish in-distribution from out-of-distribution samples, enabling OOD detection.
The memorization-generalization trade-off is controlled by regularization strength, such as bottleneck dimension.
papers.limitation: The method is primarily demonstrated on autoencoders; extension to other architectures (e.g., SSL models, LLMs) requires further analysis.
future_direction: Study latent vector fields in models beyond autoencoders, such as self-supervised learning models and large language models.
Investigate the impact of architectural elements (e.g., positional embeddings) on the latent dynamics.
Explore the connection between latent dynamics and reasoning in models.
papers.abstract: Neural networks transform high-dimensional data into compact, structured representations, often modeled as elements of a lower dimensional latent space. In this paper, we present an alternative interpretation of neural models as dynamical systems acting on the latent manifold. Specifically, we show that autoencoder models implicitly define a latent vector field on the manifold, derived by iteratively applying the encoding-decoding map, without any additional training. We observe that standard training procedures introduce inductive biases that lead to the emergence of attractor points within this vector field. Drawing on this insight, we propose to leverage the vector field as a representation for the network, providing a novel tool to analyze the properties of the model and the data. This representation enables to: (i) analyze the generalization and memorization regimes of neural models, even throughout training; (ii) extract prior knowledge encoded in the network's parameters from the attractors, without requiring any input data; (iii) identify out-of-distribution samples from their trajectories in the vector field. We further validate our approach on vision foundation models, showcasing the applicability and effectiveness of our method in real-world scenarios.

papers.title: The Computational Complexity of Circuit Discovery for Inner Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the computational complexity of circuit discovery queries for inner interpretability in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a complexity analysis of circuit discovery queries, showing that many are intractable (NP-hard, Σp2-hard, etc.), but also identifies tractable relaxations such as quasi-minimal circuits.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that circuit discovery for inner interpretability is computationally challenging, but identifies tractable relaxations and provides a framework for understanding the complexity of interpretability queries.
papers.key_findings:
Many circuit discovery queries (e.g., sufficient circuit, circuit ablation) are NP-hard or Σp2-hard.
Some queries remain fixed-parameter intractable (W[1]-hard) even when parameterizing by model depth or other features.
Some queries are inapproximable under additive, multiplicative, and probabilistic approximation schemes.
There is a formal separation between local and global query complexity, which helps explain interpretability illusions.
Quasi-minimal circuit queries are tractable (PTIME) and retain useful affordances for description and control.
future_direction: Empirical and formal characterization of learned weights to inform average-case analyses.
Exploring more parameters for fixed-parameter tractability in circuit discovery queries.
Designing queries that rely on mid-level abstractions to bridge circuits and human-intelligible algorithms.
papers.abstract: Many proposed applications of neural networks in machine learning, cognitive/brain science, and society hinge on the feasibility of inner interpretability via circuit discovery. This calls for empirical and theoretical explorations of viable algorithmic options. Despite advances in the design and testing of heuristics, there are concerns about their scalability and faithfulness at a time when we lack understanding of the complexity properties of the problems they are deployed to solve. To address this, we study circuit discovery with classical and parameterized computational complexity theory: (1) we describe a conceptual scaffolding to reason about circuit finding queries in terms of affordances for description, explanation, prediction and control; (2) we formalize a comprehensive set of queries for mechanistic explanation, and propose a formal framework for their analysis; (3) we use it to settle the complexity of many query variants and relaxations of practical interest on multi-layer perceptrons. Our findings reveal a challenging complexity landscape. Many queries are intractable, remain fixed-parameter intractable relative to model/circuit features, and inapproximable under additive, multiplicative, and probabilistic approximation schemes. To navigate this landscape, we prove there exist transformations to tackle some of these hard problems with better-understood heuristics, and prove the tractability or fixed-parameter tractability of more modest queries which retain useful affordances. This framework allows us to understand the scope and limits of interpretability queries, explore viable options, and compare their resource demands on existing and future architectures.

papers.title: The Dynamics of Neural Populations Capture the Laws of the Mind
papers.research_question: What would it mean to explain the mind in neural terms? The paper investigates how the dynamics of neural populations can capture the laws of the mind.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes that neural population dynamics, described as attractor states in low-dimensional feature spaces, form a privileged level of description for cognition, where macroscopic patterns enslave microscopic neural activity, and that networks of such dynamics constitute neural cognitive architectures.
papers.conclusion: The dynamics of neural populations form a privileged level of description at which the laws of behavior and cognition manifest themselves, and this level cannot be eliminated by reduction to a more microscopic level.
papers.key_findings:
Neural populations are a privileged level of description to understand cognition and behavior.
Neural dynamics at the population level generate stable attractor states that serve as representations.
Cognition unfolds as sequences of stable neural states are autonomously generated by neural dynamical systems that go through instabilities.
Networks of neural dynamics constitute neural cognitive architectures that enable increasingly complex forms of cognition.
The reduction of mind to neural mechanisms should follow the non-equilibrium physics metaphor, where macroscopic neural states enslave microscopic neural activity.
papers.limitation:
The separation of scales between macroscopic neural dynamics and microscopic neural activity might be broken by complex nonlinear processes that reach across spatial and temporal scales.
The paper does not cover how macroscopic neural dynamics are re-shaped by experience through neural mechanisms of learning.
future_direction: Address how macroscopic neural dynamics are re-shaped by experience through neural mechanisms of learning.
Explore scale-free theories that avoid reductive elimination of the macroscopic scale.
papers.abstract: What would it mean to explain the mind in neural terms? Neural accounts of the mind are often sought in a reductionistic spirit in which neural mechanisms explain cognition. Because an individual's thoughts and behaviors are not reproducible without careful control of task, stimulus, and behavioral history, laws of the mind are the currency of psychology. Reduction may thus have to take the form familiar from physics: deriving macroscopic laws from microscopic laws. I argue that the metaphor of reduction from non-equilibrium physics may be the most appropriate. Macroscopic patterns of neural activity, which cause behavior and thought, are slow dynamical variables that dominate the fast microscopic dynamics of individual neurons and synapses. I outline a theoretical framework in which strongly recurrent neural networks, described by neural dynamics, generate neural representations as attractor states that are embedded in low-dimensional feature spaces. Instabilities of these states are instrumental in decision-making and the generation of sequences of mental states that are the basis for higher cognition. Networks of such neural population dynamics form neural cognitive architectures that capture the laws of the mind.

papers.title: MindCraft: How Concept Trees Take Shape In Deep Models
papers.research_question: How do neural networks internally construct and consolidate abstract concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the MindCraft framework and Concept Trees to systematically trace how abstract concepts emerge, branch, and stabilize across layers in deep models.
papers.conclusion: MindCraft provides a hierarchical reconstruction of a model's reasoning process, offering a significant step towards building transparent, interpretable, and accountable AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Concept Trees reveal a hierarchical, tree-shaped organization of concept separation within models, with more salient concepts branching earlier.
The method captures conceptual importance shaped by context, not just token embedding distances.
Propagation patterns of counterfactual differences are consistent across diverse tasks, indicating a robust hierarchical dynamic.
Concept separation layers are disentangled from input embedding distances, highlighting the framework's ability to analyze high-level conceptual organization.
The framework is applicable across multiple model architectures and scales, demonstrating generality.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to multi-modal domains.
Using the identified Concept Paths to perform precise, surgical edits on model behavior.
Exploring the compositional 'algebra' of how multiple concepts interact within the network's learned representation space.
papers.abstract: Large-scale foundation models demonstrate strong performance across language, vision, and reasoning tasks. However, how they internally structure and stabilize concepts remains elusive. Inspired by causal inference, we introduce the MindCraft framework built upon Concept Trees. By applying spectral decomposition at each layer and linking principal directions into branching Concept Paths, Concept Trees reconstruct the hierarchical emergence of concepts, revealing exactly when they diverge from shared representations into linearly separable subspaces. Empirical evaluations across diverse scenarios across disciplines, including medical diagnosis, physics reasoning, and political decision-making, show that Concept Trees recover semantic hierarchies, disentangle latent concepts, and can be widely applied across multiple domains. The Concept Tree establishes a widely applicable and powerful framework that enables in-depth analysis of conceptual representations in deep models, marking a significant step forward in the foundation of interpretable AI.

papers.title: Explanatory models in neuroscience: Part 1 -- taking mechanistic abstraction seriously
papers.research_question: What criteria must neural network models satisfy to be considered mechanistic explanations of brain function?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the 3M++ criteria, which expand the notion of model-to-mechanism mapping to show that deep neural networks can serve as abstract mechanistic models of brain function when they are runnable and mappable via similarity transforms.
papers.conclusion: Deep neural networks can be good mechanistic models of brain function when assessed with the 3M++ criteria, and the appropriate level of abstraction is key to their explanatory power.
papers.key_findings:
The 3M++ criteria require a model to be a 'runnable abstraction' and to be mappable to the brain using similarity transforms (like linear transforms).
Deep neural networks, when trained for object recognition, can satisfy the 3M++ criteria and thus serve as mechanistic models of the primate ventral visual pathway.
The abstractions used in DNNs (e.g., Linear-Nonlinear units) are the same as those already employed in experimental neuroscience.
The mapping between DNN layers and brain areas can be performed using linear transforms, analogous to mapping neural responses across individuals.
The level of abstraction is crucial; DNNs operate at the spike-rate level, which is a self-consistent and predictively adequate level for explaining visual processing.
papers.limitation: HCNNs do not explain 100% of the stimulus-driven variability of ventral pathway neurons, up to the inter-animal noise ceiling.
future_direction: Developing improved models (e.g., with recurrent and feedback connections) to achieve 100% statistical accuracy in mapping to the visual system.
Exploring the relationship between optimization and intelligibility, as addressed in the companion paper.
papers.abstract: Despite the recent success of neural network models in mimicking animal performance on visual perceptual tasks, critics worry that these models fail to illuminate brain function. We take it that a central approach to explanation in systems neuroscience is that of mechanistic modeling, where understanding the system is taken to require fleshing out the parts, organization, and activities of a system, and how those give rise to behaviors of interest. However, it remains somewhat controversial what it means for a model to describe a mechanism, and whether neural network models qualify as explanatory. We argue that certain kinds of neural network models are actually good examples of mechanistic models, when the right notion of mechanistic mapping is deployed. Building on existing work on model-to-mechanism mapping (3M), we describe criteria delineating such a notion, which we call 3M++. These criteria require us, first, to identify a level of description that is both abstract but detailed enough to be "runnable", and then, to construct model-to-brain mappings using the same principles as those employed for brain-to-brain mapping across individuals. Perhaps surprisingly, the abstractions required are those already in use in experimental neuroscience, and are of the kind deployed in the construction of more familiar computational models, just as the principles of inter-brain mappings are very much in the spirit of those already employed in the collection and analysis of data across animals. In a companion paper, we address the relationship between optimization and intelligibility, in the context of functional evolutionary explanations. Taken together, mechanistic interpretations of computational models and the dependencies between form and function illuminated by optimization processes can help us to understand why brain systems are built they way they are.

papers.title: Representing Neural Network Layers as Linear Operations via Koopman Operator Theory
papers.research_question: Can we linearize individual layers of a neural network using Koopman operator theory and delay-coordinates embedding, and how does this affect model performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to linearize individual layers of a neural network using Koopman operator theory and delay-coordinates embedding, achieving performance close to the original network.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that Koopman theory and delay-coordinates embedding can linearize individual neural network layers while retaining performance, offering a new perspective for understanding and controlling networks.
papers.key_findings:
Delay-coordinates embedding (Hankelization) is an effective observable function for linearizing neural network layers via Koopman theory.
Replacing layers with a linear DMD model retains high accuracy: up to 97.3% on Yin-Yang (vs 98.4% original) and up to 95.8% on MNIST (vs 97.2% original).
The success of layer replacement varies by layer; replacing the final hidden layer is most successful, suggesting it performs a simpler transformation.
Increasing the delay parameter and number of trajectories improves the DMD model's performance.
Eigenvalue and singular vector analysis shows that delay embedding linearizes the dynamics, as seen in simpler sinusoidal patterns in singular vectors.
papers.limitation: The maximum delay parameter is limited by the number of scaling layers, which restricts the exploration of delay parameters.
future_direction: Analyze the learned eigenmodes and eigenvalues to understand their relationship with layer replacement success.
Develop methods to edit trained models in the Koopman space.
Extend the framework to other architectures like convolutional or attention layers.
papers.abstract: The strong performance of simple neural networks is often attributed to their nonlinear activations. However, a linear view of neural networks makes understanding and controlling networks much more approachable. We draw from a dynamical systems view of neural networks, offering a fresh perspective by using Koopman operator theory and its connections with dynamic mode decomposition (DMD). Together, they offer a framework for linearizing dynamical systems by embedding the system into an appropriate observable space. By reframing a neural network as a dynamical system, we demonstrate that we can replace the nonlinear layer in a pretrained multi-layer perceptron (MLP) with a finite-dimensional linear operator. In addition, we analyze the eigenvalues of DMD and the right singular vectors of SVD, to present evidence that time-delayed coordinates provide a straightforward and highly effective observable space for Koopman theory to linearize a network layer. Consequently, we replace layers of an MLP trained on the Yin-Yang dataset with predictions from a DMD model, achieving a mdoel accuracy of up to 97.3%, compared to the original 98.4%. In addition, we replace layers in an MLP trained on the MNIST dataset, achieving up to 95.8%, compared to the original 97.2% on the test set.

papers.title: Deep Manifold Part 2: Neural Network Mathematics
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether data is inherently high-order nonlinear and whether neural networks are fundamentally a numerical computation framework.
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a mathematical framework for neural networks as learnable numerical computation shaped by manifold complexity, high-order nonlinearity, and boundary conditions.
papers.conclusion: The Deep Manifold framework opens a new mathematical window into understanding neural networks, and its validity rests on two foundational questions: whether data is inherently high-order nonlinear and whether neural networks are fundamentally a numerical computation framework.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks are learnable numerical computations shaped by manifold complexity, high-order nonlinearity, and boundary conditions.
Neural networks operate as stacked piecewise manifolds, with dynamic node covers and coordinate changes that provide data efficiency.
The fixed-point residual is the primitive equation of neural networks, and training minimizes this residual to stabilize representations.
Real-world data complexity (high-order nonlinearity, infinite scope, stochasticity) constrains learnability and explains why capability emerges only when fixed-point regions stabilize.
The framework suggests that distributed systems of small elastic models (manifold federation) are a natural extension to overcome limitations of monolithic models.
papers.limitation:
Human perception is limited, and models trained on human data inherit this perceptual boundary, learning the world-as-seen-by-humans rather than reality itself.
Digital representations of the real world (e.g., RGB images, sensor data) introduce information loss, distortions, and artifacts, constraining what models can learn.
future_direction: Developing a mosaic of small elastic models (SLMs) that capture local pieces of the manifold to avoid error compounding in monolithic models.
Exploring federated learning as distributed manifold alignment, where local models align through boundary consistency without sharing data.
Building agentic AI systems based on the Federation Triangle (Model, Agent, Tool) to solve problems through fixed-point composition across distributed operators.
papers.abstract: This work develops the global equations of neural networks through stacked piecewise manifolds, fixed-point theory, and boundary-conditioned iteration. Once fixed coordinates and operators are removed, a neural network appears as a learnable numerical computation shaped by manifold complexity, high-order nonlinearity, and boundary conditions. Real-world data impose strong data complexity, near-infinite scope, scale, and minibatch fragmentation, while training dynamics produce learning complexity through shifting node covers, curvature accumulation, and the rise and decay of plasticity. These forces constrain learnability and explain why capability emerges only when fixed-point regions stabilize. Neural networks do not begin with fixed points; they construct them through residual-driven iteration. This perspective clarifies the limits of monolithic models under geometric and data-induced plasticity and motivates architectures and federated systems that distribute manifold complexity across many elastic models, forming a coherent world-modeling framework grounded in geometry, algebra, fixed points, and real-data complexity.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models by resolving superposition, and can these features be used for causal analysis and circuit discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders provide a scalable, unsupervised method to find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models, enabling precise causal analysis and circuit discovery.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders are a scalable, unsupervised approach to disentangling language model features from superposition, facilitating interpretability, circuit mapping, and targeted model editing.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoder features are more interpretable than neurons, PCA, ICA, and random directions as measured by autointerpretability scores.
Sparse autoencoder features allow more precise localization of causally important features for the IOI task than PCA, requiring fewer patches to achieve a given KL divergence.
Individual features are monosemantic (e.g., an apostrophe feature) and have predictable effects on output logits, such as suppressing the 's' token after an apostrophe.
Sparse autoencoders enable automatic circuit detection across layers, as demonstrated for a closing parenthesis feature.
The method works well on residual stream activations but has limitations for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
papers.limitation:
The autoencoders do not achieve zero reconstruction loss, indicating they fail to capture all information in the activations.
Replacing activations with reconstructions increases perplexity, showing loss of information.
The method is less robust for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
Autointerpretability has limitations, such as GPT-4 struggling with patterns centered around next or previous tokens.
future_direction: Explore other sparse autoencoder architectures and minimize change in model outputs when replacing activations.
Incorporate information about model weights or dictionary features from adjacent layers into training.
Improve feature discovery in MLP and attention layers, and generalize to other tasks and behaviors.
papers.abstract: One of the roadblocks to a better understanding of neural networks' internals is \textit{polysemanticity}, where neurons appear to activate in multiple, semantically distinct contexts. Polysemanticity prevents us from identifying concise, human-understandable explanations for what neural networks are doing internally. One hypothesised cause of polysemanticity is \textit{superposition}, where neural networks represent more features than they have neurons by assigning features to an overcomplete set of directions in activation space, rather than to individual neurons. Here, we attempt to identify those directions, using sparse autoencoders to reconstruct the internal activations of a language model. These autoencoders learn sets of sparsely activating features that are more interpretable and monosemantic than directions identified by alternative approaches, where interpretability is measured by automated methods. Moreover, we show that with our learned set of features, we can pinpoint the features that are causally responsible for counterfactual behaviour on the indirect object identification task \citep{wang2022interpretability} to a finer degree than previous decompositions. This work indicates that it is possible to resolve superposition in language models using a scalable, unsupervised method. Our method may serve as a foundation for future mechanistic interpretability work, which we hope will enable greater model transparency and steerability.

papers.title: The Non-Linear Representation Dilemma: Is Causal Abstraction Enough for Mechanistic Interpretability?
papers.research_question: Is causal abstraction sufficient for mechanistic interpretability when alignment maps are not constrained to be linear?
papers.core_contribution: Causal abstraction becomes vacuous when alignment maps are allowed to be arbitrarily complex, leading to the non-linear representation dilemma where there is no principled way to balance map complexity and accuracy.
papers.conclusion: Causal abstraction is not enough for mechanistic interpretability without assumptions about how models encode information.
papers.key_findings:
Theoretically, any algorithm can be perfectly mapped to any neural network under reasonable assumptions if alignment maps are arbitrarily complex.
Empirically, non-linear alignment maps can achieve near-perfect interchange intervention accuracy even on randomly initialized models that do not solve the task.
The complexity of alignment maps needed to achieve perfect IIA decreases as the model trains.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical result relies on assumptions such as input-injectivity and output-surjectivity of the neural network.
Empirical alignment map training can suffer from grokking and requires careful hyperparameter tuning.
future_direction: Studying the connection between information-encoding assumptions and causal abstraction.
papers.abstract: The concept of causal abstraction got recently popularised to demystify the opaque decision-making processes of machine learning models; in short, a neural network can be abstracted as a higher-level algorithm if there exists a function which allows us to map between them. Notably, most interpretability papers implement these maps as linear functions, motivated by the linear representation hypothesis: the idea that features are encoded linearly in a model's representations. However, this linearity constraint is not required by the definition of causal abstraction. In this work, we critically examine the concept of causal abstraction by considering arbitrarily powerful alignment maps. In particular, we prove that under reasonable assumptions, any neural network can be mapped to any algorithm, rendering this unrestricted notion of causal abstraction trivial and uninformative. We complement these theoretical findings with empirical evidence, demonstrating that it is possible to perfectly map models to algorithms even when these models are incapable of solving the actual task; e.g., on an experiment using randomly initialised language models, our alignment maps reach 100\% interchange-intervention accuracy on the indirect object identification task. This raises the non-linear representation dilemma: if we lift the linearity constraint imposed to alignment maps in causal abstraction analyses, we are left with no principled way to balance the inherent trade-off between these maps' complexity and accuracy. Together, these results suggest an answer to our title's question: causal abstraction is not enough for mechanistic interpretability, as it becomes vacuous without assumptions about how models encode information. Studying the connection between this information-encoding assumption and causal abstraction should lead to exciting future work.

papers.title: Position-aware Automatic Circuit Discovery
papers.research_question: How can we incorporate positional information into automatic circuit discovery for language models to address limitations of position-agnostic methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces position-aware circuit discovery (PEAP) and dataset schemas to enable fully automated discovery of position-sensitive circuits, achieving better faithfulness than position-agnostic methods.
papers.conclusion: Position-aware circuit discovery and schemas improve circuit faithfulness and enable automated analysis of variable-length inputs, providing a more precise foundation for mechanistic explanations.
papers.key_findings:
Position-aware circuits are smaller and more faithful than position-agnostic circuits.
Automatically generated schemas (with or without saliency masks) yield circuits comparable to those from human-designed schemas.
The proposed method handles variable-length inputs via schemas, enabling circuit discovery in more naturalistic settings.
papers.limitation:
Schemas assume sequential order of spans, which may not hold for all datasets.
The schema generation and application pipeline may not always produce valid schemas for all examples.
future_direction: Relax the sequential order assumption in schemas to support greater variation across examples.
Investigate the components in the circuit for the Winobias task to understand the balance between task-relevant and bias-inducing factors.

papers.title: Phase transition encoded in neural network
papers.research_question: How do temperature-supervised neural networks capture information of phase transition and what physical quantities do they learn?
papers.core_contribution: Temperature-supervised neural networks encode phase transition information in their weights, learning either magnetization or internal energy as features depending on network architecture and prediction accuracy.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks trained to predict temperature encode phase transition information in their weights, and the extracted physical quantity (magnetization or energy) depends on the network architecture and training accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
The fully-connected neural network learns magnetization from input spin configurations, and its weights show a drastic change at the critical temperature, enabling phase transition detection.
The convolutional neural network learns internal energy, achieves higher temperature prediction accuracy, and its weights are proportional to free energy, encoding phase transition information more implicitly.
The phase transition information is captured in the neural network weights even without explicit supervision of phase labels.
The accuracy of temperature prediction is theoretically bounded by the overlap of energy probability distributions at different temperatures.
Convolutional networks perform better because they capture spatial correlations, leading to learning internal energy rather than magnetization.
papers.limitation:
The method may not correctly detect phase transitions driven by different physical mechanisms such as Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) transitions or topological phase transitions.
The fully-connected network only distinguishes between ordered and disordered phases and cannot predict fine-grained temperatures within each phase.
The accuracy of temperature prediction is limited by the overlap of energy distributions at different temperatures in finite systems.
papers.abstract: Abstract We discuss an aspect of neural networks for the purpose of phase transition detection. To this end, we first train the neural network by feeding Ising/Potts configurations with labels of temperature so that it can predict the temperature of the input. We do not explicitly supervise whether the configurations are in the ordered/disordered phase. Nevertheless, we can identify the critical temperature from the parameters (weights and biases) of the trained neural network. We attempt to understand how temperature-supervised neural networks capture information on the phase transition by paying attention to what quantities they learn. Our detailed analyses reveal that they learn different physical quantities depending on how well they are trained. The main observation in this study is how the weights in the trained neural network can have information on the phase transition in addition to temperature.

papers.title: A Unified Theory of Sparse Dictionary Learning in Mechanistic Interpretability: Piecewise Biconvexity and Spurious Minima
papers.research_question: Why do sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, and what is the theoretical understanding of these phenomena?
papers.core_contribution: Develops a unified theoretical framework for sparse dictionary learning (SDL) that explains failure modes like feature absorption and dead neurons via piecewise biconvex optimization and non-identifiability, and proposes feature anchoring to improve feature recovery.
papers.conclusion: The theoretical framework explains persistent failure modes in SDL methods, and feature anchoring provides an effective, method-agnostic technique to improve feature recovery by reducing underdetermination.
papers.key_findings:
SDL optimization exhibits piecewise biconvex structure, enabling analysis of its landscape.
SDL suffers from non-identifiability, leading to spurious minima that result in polysemantic features.
Feature absorption arises naturally from hierarchical concept structures and corresponds to partial minima.
Feature anchoring, which constrains a subset of features to known directions, significantly improves feature recovery across SDL methods.
Dead neuron resampling helps escape spurious local minima in large language models.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical analysis relies on the Linear Representation Hypothesis, which assumes features are linear directions; this may not hold for all representations.
The synthetic benchmark, while controlled, may not capture all complexities of real-world data.
Feature anchoring requires anchor features, which may be difficult to obtain in some settings.
future_direction: Extending the theory to non-linear representations.
Applying feature anchoring to more domains and real-world tasks.
Integrating anchoring with other SDL improvements and scaling to larger models.
papers.abstract: As AI models achieve remarkable capabilities across diverse domains, understanding what representations they learn and how they encode concepts has become increasingly important for both scientific progress and trustworthy deployment. Recent works in mechanistic interpretability have widely reported that neural networks represent meaningful concepts as linear directions in their representation spaces and often encode diverse concepts in superposition. Various sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods, including sparse autoencoders, transcoders, and crosscoders, are utilized to address this by training auxiliary models with sparsity constraints to disentangle these superposed concepts into monosemantic features. These methods are the backbone of modern mechanistic interpretability, yet in practice they consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, with very limited theoretical understanding of why these phenomena occur. Existing theoretical work is limited to tied-weight sparse autoencoders, leaving the broader family of SDL methods without formal grounding. We develop the first unified theoretical framework that casts all major SDL variants as a single piecewise biconvex optimization problem, and characterize its global solution set, non-identifiability, and spurious optima. This analysis yields principled explanations for feature absorption and dead neurons. To expose these pathologies under full ground-truth access, we introduce the Linear Representation Bench. Guided by our theory, we propose feature anchoring, a novel technique that restores SDL identifiability, substantially improving feature recovery across synthetic benchmarks and real neural representations.

papers.title: Universal Redundancies in Time Series Foundation Models
papers.research_question: What mechanisms enable TSFMs to construct effective zero-shot forecasts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds universal redundancies in Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs), shows that middle layers are highly redundant and models are robust to ablations, and introduces an intrinsic head-pruning strategy based on stable rank to identify heads responsible for context parroting and seasonality bias.
papers.conclusion: The study sheds light on universal properties of TSFMs, revealing redundancies and providing an intrinsic head-pruning strategy that identifies heads responsible for common failure modes.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers in TSFMs are highly redundant and can be ablated with minimal performance drop.
An intrinsic head pruning strategy based on the stable rank of query-key projection matrices effectively identifies important heads.
Specific attention heads are responsible for degenerate phenomena such as context parroting and seasonality bias.
TSFMs exhibit significant variation in sensitivity to MLP ablations across architectures, with encoder-decoder models being more resilient.
The first and last layers are most important for model performance.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical framework is technically limited to encoder-decoder models with causal masking.
The intrinsic head pruning strategy cannot account for the data-dependent exponential tilt term in the attention mechanism.
future_direction: Investigating how architecture determines what the transformer loads onto MLPs versus attention heads.
papers.abstract: Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) leverage extensive pretraining to accurately predict unseen time series during inference, without the need for task-specific fine-tuning. Through large-scale evaluations on standard benchmarks, we find that leading transformer-based TSFMs exhibit redundant components in their intermediate layers. We introduce a set of tools for mechanistic interpretability of TSFMs, including ablations of specific components and direct logit attribution on the residual stream. Our findings are consistent across several leading TSFMs with diverse architectures, and across a diverse set of real-world and synthetic time-series datasets. We discover that all models in our study are robust to ablations of entire layers. Furthermore, we develop a theoretical framework framing transformers as kernel regressors, motivating a purely intrinsic strategy for ablating heads based on the stable rank of the per-head projection matrices. Using this approach, we uncover the specific heads responsible for degenerate phenomena widely observed in TSFMs, such as parroting of motifs from the context and seasonality bias. Our study sheds light on the universal properties of this emerging class of architectures for continuous-time sequence modeling.

papers.title: Quality of internal representation shapes learning performance in feedback neural networks
papers.research_question: How does the interplay between internal network dynamics and target properties shape learning performance in feedback neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Learning performance in feedback networks is maximized when the target frequency matches a resonance frequency determined by internal connectivity, corresponding to high-dimensional and desynchronized internal representations.
papers.conclusion: The quality of internal representation, shaped by the interplay between network connectivity and target dynamics, is a major determinant of learning success in feedback networks.
papers.key_findings:
Learning performance in feedback networks is non-monotonic with target frequency, with an optimal frequency that decreases with increasing connectivity strength.
The optimal frequency corresponds to a resonance where the internal representation has maximal dimensionality and minimal synchrony.
The condition number of the cross-correlation matrix is minimized at the resonance frequency, making learning more robust.
These findings hold across different training algorithms (LS, ridge, RLS) and for both linear and non-linear networks.
In non-linear networks, the resonance frequency increases with target amplitude.
papers.abstract: The authors find a resonance frequency at which feedback neural networks reproduce a sinusoidal wave, and show that network performance is determined by the robustness of the corresponding internal representation.

papers.title: The Few Govern the Many:Unveiling Few-Layer Dominance for Time Series Models
papers.research_question: Why do larger time series models not always perform better (scaling paradox), and what is the root cause?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a scaling paradox in time series models where larger models do not perform better, discovers that only a few layers are functionally important (few-layer dominance), and proposes a pruning method to retain these critical layers, achieving comparable or better performance with fewer parameters and faster inference.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that few-layer dominance is a key phenomenon in time series models, and pruning redundant layers can lead to efficient and high-performing models.
papers.key_findings:
Scaling paradox is pervasive in time series models: larger models do not necessarily achieve better performance.
The root cause is few-layer dominance: only a small subset of layers are functionally important, while others are redundant.
Retaining only the critical layers (e.g., 21% of parameters) can achieve superior performance, faster inference, and up to 12% accuracy improvement.
The pruning method is universal and works on 8 SOTA models, retaining less than 30% of layers achieves comparable or superior accuracy in over 95% of tasks.
Increasing data volume or diversity does not alleviate the scaling paradox.
future_direction: Incorporate few-layer dominance into architectural design of large-scale time series models.
papers.abstract: Large-scale models are at the forefront of time series (TS) forecasting, dominated by two paradigms: fine-tuning text-based Large Language Models (LLM4TS) and training Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) from scratch. Both approaches share a foundational assumption that scaling up model capacity and data volume leads to improved performance. However, we observe a \textit{\textbf{scaling paradox}} in TS models, revealing a puzzling phenomenon that larger models do \emph{NOT} achieve better performance. Through extensive experiments on two model families across four scales (100M to 1.7B parameters) and diverse data (up to 6B observations), we rigorously confirm that the scaling paradox is a pervasive issue. We then diagnose its root cause by analyzing internal representations, identifying a phenomenon we call \textit{few-layer dominance}: only a small subset of layers are functionally important, while the majority are redundant, under-utilized, and can even distract training. Based on this discovery, we propose a practical method to automatically identify and retain only these dominant layers. In our models, retaining only 21\% of the parameters achieves up to a 12\% accuracy improvement and a 2.7$\times$ inference speedup. We validate the universality of our method on 8 prominent SOTA models (LLM4TS and TSFMs, 90M to 6B), showing that retaining less than 30\% of layers achieves comparable or superior accuracy in over 95\% of tasks.

papers.title: Moirai-MoE: Empowering Time Series Foundation Models with Sparse Mixture of Experts
papers.research_question: How can time series foundation models achieve effective unified training by moving from human-imposed frequency-level specialization to automatic token-level specialization using sparse mixture of experts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MOIRAI-MOE, a time series foundation model that uses a single input/output projection layer and delegates pattern modeling to sparse mixture of experts, enabling automatic token-level specialization and improving forecasting performance.
papers.conclusion: MOIRAI-MOE is an effective approach for time series foundation models, achieving token-level specialization and superior performance in forecasting tasks.
papers.key_findings:
MOIRAI-MOE outperforms existing foundation models (TimesFM, Chronos, MOIRAI) in both in-distribution and zero-shot forecasting.
The decoder-only training objective is more efficient than the masked encoder approach.
The proposed token clustering gating function outperforms linear projection gating variants.
Model analysis shows that MOIRAI-MOE produces frequency-invariant representations in deeper layers.
Expert allocation reflects time series periodicity patterns, indicating token-level specialization.
future_direction: Pruning underutilized experts for model compression
papers.abstract: Time series foundation models have demonstrated impressive performance as zero-shot forecasters.
